_README: Source citations removed from rendered route prose — the NO SOURCES ANYWHERE IN THE APP rule.
Every value here is the row's ORIGINAL text with attribution deleted and the grammar repaired.
Each batch was produced by literal find/replace against the original with every pattern asserted
to match, so untouched prose is byte-identical rather than retyped, and each was checked by
verifysrc.mjs: no citation survives, every number and every capitalised word in the new text
already appears in the old, and nothing collapsed below 55% without a declared reason.
First-ascent history is deliberately KEPT — Fred Beckey wrote the guidebook and made half these
first ascents, and deleting the ascent record would be a worse defect than the one being fixed.

set.descent_text: A Servant to Liberty (earlier known as 'A Slave to Liberty') climbs the first three pitches of Freedom or Death (5.10, 5.11, 5.11), then steps right to join Thin Red Line for its upper pitches. Descent therefore follows Thin Red Line's exit: rappel with two ropes off M&M Ledge (fixed pin/wire anchor), then move climber's-left to bolted anchors for four double-rope rappels back to the base — five rappels total, all on bolted stations.

Abernathy Peak's North Ridge is a scramble, not a technical roped climb, and no fixed rappel anchors exist on this route — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb/scramble the class 3 ridge crest north back to the 7,680+ ft saddle (the route's crux terrain, with a couple of noticeably 'intense' exposed spots — face in and downclimb deliberately here, since the same loose, eroded rock that's manageable going up is more consequential coming down). From the saddle, pick your way back down the loose scree and talus — solid footing near the saddle gives way to looser scree lower down, similar in character to the neighboring, more-traveled Scatter Lake route where parties commonly plunge-step the scree comfortably once clear of the rockier upper band. Continue down to the mine trail and the North Creek crossing, then rejoin North Creek Trail #413 for the hike back to the trailhead. This is a 0-rappel walk-off/downclimb in normal summer conditions — no rope, rack, or anchors needed. Parties who ascended on firm early-season snow should be ready to descend the upper slopes via glissade or a controlled snow descent with an ice axe instead of scree, and should watch for rockfall from parties above given the generally loose rock on this route.

set.beta: Described as the recommended route: gain Asa Peak's Northeast Ridge, traverse to Agnes's south ridge, and climb short technical sections up to 5.6-5.8. From a high camp near Icy-Spruce Pass, parties make a rising traverse over snow, talus, and slabs to the south ridge crest south of Point 7760, then rope up for several pitches of Class 4-5 rock on or left of the crest. Where the crest gets too craggy, downclimb one pitch to a ledge system and traverse to a whaleback with views of the summit block. From the 7,480-ft south col, traverse a high snowpatch and ascend a broad Class 2-3 ramp just left of a snow-filled gully, dog-legging right to a headwall; a 5.8 chimney (the crux) and one more roped pitch lead to a final ~100-ft Class 2-3 scramble to the summit.

set.approach: Start at the High Bridge Guard Station & Campground on Stehekin Valley Road (elev. ~1,600 ft) — reached from Stehekin by the NPS shuttle bus (about 11.3 miles) or on foot, since there is no through road; Stehekin itself is reached only by the Lady of the Lake/Lady Express ferry up Lake Chelan or by floatplane. From High Bridge, follow the Agnes Creek Trail (PCT southbound) up the valley through old-growth forest, a well-graded trail passing Three-Mile Camp and reaching Swamp Creek Camp at about mile 8.5 (roughly 5 hours for a loaded pack). Continue up-trail toward Mile 10, then leave the maintained tread to find a log crossing of Agnes Creek — the historic log is reportedly long gone, so scout for a currently-usable log or ford near Mile 10 — followed shortly by a second log crossing of Spruce Creek. From the far bank of Spruce Creek, the route turns into a steep, brushy, off-trail climb north/northwest up the hillside: plan on gaining the first ~1,000 vertical feet through thick slide alder, brush, and scrub trees, which is by far the slowest and most punishing part of the day. The brush eases noticeably above ~4,000 ft, and the cross-country line continues up open slabs and heather to "Upper Blue Basin," a rock-and-heather bench that serves as the standard high camp (figure on a very long day — roughly 10 hours from Swamp Creek Camp to camp in July). Water is reliable at Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek during the approach but is not guaranteed again until snowmelt/tarns near Upper Blue Basin, so top off before starting the brush climb. From high camp, the climb proper begins by crossing Icy–Spruce Pass and making a rising traverse over snow, talus, and rock slabs to reach the crest of Agnes' south ridge just south of Point 7760, where roped Class 4–5 rock leads up the ridge. Key hazards: creek crossings that vary year to year and may require route-finding to locate a safe log or ford, sustained steep brush with real potential to get off-route, and no maintained trail or cairns once you leave the Agnes Creek Trail. The standard line follows Asa Peak's northeast ridge onto Agnes' south ridge before the roped class 4-5 pitches begin.

set.beta: From the Rachel Lake / Lila Lake trail junction, an unsigned 'climber's path' marked by a cairn leaves the maintained trail and climbs Alta Mountain's south ridge. The initial section is steep with loose rock and large steps and no shade; the grade then moderates onto a knife-edge ridge with sustained exposure. There are several class 2-3 moves, at least one 6-8 ft near-vertical step with good holds but serious exposure, a class 3 downclimb crux near the top, and multiple false summits before the true summit is reached. The route is non-technical (no rope typically used) but is exposed enough to be unsuitable for anyone uneasy with heights or for dogs.
set.approach: From the Rachel Lake Trailhead (2,800 ft, end of FS Rd 4930 off Kachess Lake Rd, Exit 62 from I-90), start on Rachel Lake Trail #1313. The first ~2.75 miles follow Box Canyon Creek on gentle grade, crossing several side streams and cascades (reliable water throughout — no need to carry much from the car). At about mile 2.75 the trail crosses Box/Canyon Creek and hits the notorious 'mile from hell': a heavily rooted, rocky boot-beaten climb that gains roughly 1,300 ft in about a mile, with large step-ups and no switchbacks — this is the crux of the approach fitness-wise, not technically hard but brutal with a full pack. The trail tops out at Rachel Lake (4,700 ft, ~3.5-4 mi from the TH); a use trail/climber's path branches right near the outhouse and skirts the north side of the lake, then switchbacks steeply up rocky tread for about half a mile to the Rampart Ridge crest (~5,100 ft). At the ridge junction, go left (south) for Rampart Lakes or right for Lila Lake/Alta Mountain — for this route, follow the trail south along the ridge/east side of the Rampart Lakes basin. Stay on maintained tread through the lakes basin (it's fragile alpine turf/talus; short-cut social trails are discouraged and often marked closed with sticks/rock piles). At the south end of the lakes, locate the base of a large boulder gully with cliff bands on its left (west) side; ascend this gully on a boot path to a broad saddle at about 5,570 ft on the Rampart Ridge crest. Total to this point is roughly 6-6.5 miles and ~3,000 ft gain. From the saddle, turn west and follow the increasingly exposed climber's path along the ridge crest toward Alta's summit block, negotiating three false summits, class 2-3 rock steps, and short sections of real exposure (in one section the path skirts a cliff edge — fall consequences are serious here, and the route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge). A helmet is commonly recommended for the final ridge scramble due to loose rock and exposure. Total one-way distance to the 6,274 ft summit is about 9.5-10 km (matches the on-file 19.3 km round trip) with roughly 3,300 ft of total gain.

From Winthrop, drive north on Okanogan County Road 1213 (West Chewuch Road), which becomes Forest Road 51, and follow it about 29 miles of good gravel to the Thirtymile Trailhead at road's end (3,430 ft). A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park; the free self-issue wilderness permit is at the register. Start up Chewuch Trail #510, a gentle valley trail that follows the Chewuch River for roughly 18 miles, mostly through lodgepole pine. The first five miles cross the 2001 burn — many standing snags, a bad place to be in wind — and Chewuch Falls comes at about 2.5 miles. Creek access is regular enough on the valley trail that you can refill every hour or two. Continue past the Tungsten Creek and Four Point junctions and climb out of the valley into the Cathedral Lakes basin. Car to camp at Upper Cathedral Lake (7,380 ft) is about 19.9 miles with roughly 4,900 feet of gain — essentially every party splits it over two days, with common first camps at Four Point Lake (6,850 ft) or the meadows just past Pocket Lake. Note the trail north of Four Point Creek still carries blowdown from the 2017 Diamond Creek Fire; trail crews have cut hundreds of logs out of it but conditions vary year to year. From camp on the west side of Upper Cathedral Lake, the north-wall buttresses rise directly above the water. Middle Finger Buttress is the biggest, most westerly one; walk and scramble talus and heather 15-30 minutes to its base, then traverse right to the toe of the northwest side, where a steep slab with a single thin vertical crack marks the start. Alternative trailheads: Andrews Creek (23 miles from Winthrop on the same Chewuch River Road, about 21 miles to the lakes) and Cathedral Driveway from Loomis via Toats Coulee Road.

Two common trailheads reach the base: (1) Andrews Creek Trailhead (Trail 504) — from Winthrop, take Hwy 20 to County Road 1213/West Chewuch Road, drive ~6 miles to Forest Road 51, continue ~22 miles to the trailhead at road's end (3,050 ft). Hike via Andrews Pass and the Boundary Trail to Upper Cathedral Lake (roughly 7 hours for a loaded backpacking pace). (2) Chewuch River Trail/Thirtymile Trailhead — a longer approach (about 20 miles and ~4,900 ft gain to Upper Cathedral Lake), also joining near Cathedral Pass. Most parties backpack in and camp at or near Upper Cathedral Lake (~7,380 ft) before a summit day.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the East Ridge: downclimb and scramble back through the gendarme and knife-edge sections to the notch just west of the lone gendarme where the roped climbing began. From the notch, parties either make two single-rope rappels or one longer double-rope rappel (two ropes tied together, or twin/half ropes) down steep snow to the glacier/snow slopes below rather than downclimbing the exposed step -- both are standard, established options, not just one. Anchors on this route are natural — slung horns, blocks, or small trees — supplemented by whatever tat/fixed slings a prior party left; there is no bolted station, so carry extra webcord and be ready to build or back up an anchor. Once down to the snow/talus below the notch, downclimb into the basin and reverse the long approach: back down through Porcupine Creek basin, re-ford Ingalls Creek, and climb back out over Fourth Creek Pass to the trailhead. Given the length of this descent, start it with a comfortable margin of daylight.

set.beta: In October 1992 Peter Doorish's ascent of a route on the east face of Mount Baring, with Laura Woods, went at 5.10d, and he explicitly distinguished it from his other Baring-massif routes of that season by noting that all of them except the east face ascent were Grade V climbs of about fourteen pitches. That implies a shorter, lower-commitment line — probably Grade III or IV — but there is no recorded pitch count, no length, no topo and no description of the line itself. There is no evidence of a repeat ascent. Anyone going after it should treat it as an exploratory objective: identify the line from the ground, expect the same variable gneiss and vegetated ledges as the rest of the mountain, and be self-sufficient for retreat. The east side of Baring drops toward the upper Barclay Creek drainage and is not served by any climbers' path; the practical access is over or around the peak from the standard northwest-ridge approach, or up the east-side slopes from the Barclay Creek valley.

This line is also called the "South Scramble" (3rd class, Grade II) and the Northwest Ridge Route; they are the same line. From the Barclay Lake trailhead you do not follow the maintained lake trail — you take the abandoned logging road just uphill of it, find the cairned climbers' path at the first creek crossing, and go essentially straight up the forested west side. The path gains around 2,000 feet in about a mile to reach the ridge crest near 4,000 ft, follows the ridge east, drops below a cliff band, crosses a wooded gully and traverses into a boulder-filled basin at about 4,900 ft. From the basin, cross east and climb the obvious couloir/gully about 700 feet to the notch at roughly 5,550-5,600 ft between South Baring and the main peak. Turn north out of the notch, the angle eases, and easy class-3 scrambling on heather, talus and blocky gneiss leads a final quarter mile to the 6,127-ft north summit. Aim for the north summit — the south peak is lower and harder. The outing is rated Hard at 7.0 miles round trip with 3,500 ft of gain to a 6,129-ft high point; it is elsewhere described as closer to two miles one way with 3,700 ft of gain, or roughly 4,000 ft. The discrepancy is real and reflects different start points and how much of the logging-road walk is counted; either way the defining feature is gradient, not mileage.

Established by Paul Woodrum and Peter Doorish in September 1992, Oatmeal Man was one of several routes put up on Baring's north face and the neighboring Dolomite Tower that same year (alongside Doorish's solo Right Rib, the Dolomite Tower East Corner, and the Dolomite Tower North Face route). Detailed pitch-by-pitch beta beyond the brief first-ascent record was not found.
set.approach: From US Highway 2 at milepost 42 in the town of Baring (directly across from Der Baring Store), turn north onto Barclay Creek Road, Forest Service Road 6024, cross the BNSF railroad tracks and bear left at the fork about 0.2 miles up. Follow FS 6024 roughly 4.3–4.5 miles of gravel to the Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft, where there is parking for roughly 20 cars, a vault toilet and picnic tables but no potable water. Walk Barclay Creek Trail 1055 east up the valley — it is a gentle, well-graded 2.2 miles to Barclay Lake at about 2,420 ft, directly under the wall. The north face rises straight out of the lake basin: 3,703 vertical feet from the lake to the summit in only half a mile of horizontal distance. Leave the trail near the lake and fight up the steep forested and brushy hillside beneath the wall — the first ascent of this face in 1961 found the first 1,000 feet to be exactly that kind of brush-and-forest struggle to reach a camp below the couloirs, and nothing about that terrain has improved since. There is no maintained climbers' path to the base of the main-peak wall (the fixed lines and boot track that exist on this mountain belong to the Dolomite Tower approach, which breaks off the trail well before the lake and heads up a different drainage). Allow several hours from the car to the base and expect wet vegetation, blowdown and loose ground.

Park at the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,200 ft, end of FS Road 6024/Barclay Creek Road, 4WD recommended for the last stretch), which is shared parking for the Barclay Lake hike and the unofficial Baring/Gunn Peak climbers' paths. From the trailhead, go around the outhouse/toilet and pick up an old, overgrown logging-road grade for a few hundred yards before it turns sharply uphill into a steep, muddy, eroded gully — this is the start of the unmaintained climbers' trail (look for cairns and a boot path; it is not a maintained trail and is easy to lose). The tread is very steep and often slick from the first steps, with no reliable water past the initial creek crossing, so carry what you need from the trailhead. After roughly 1 mile and about 1,800 ft of gain, the path tops out on Baring's west ridge (~4,000 ft). Follow the ridge crest generally east/southeast; there is a 2022 burn scar on the south-facing slope here, which adds loose ash and dirt underfoot and can obscure the tread — it is easy to stay too long on the crest and have to downclimb back to the correct line, so watch for where the path dips slightly below cliff bands into a wooded gully before regaining the ridge. The route then drops into a talus/boulder basin, crosses it, and climbs the main gully/talus slope up to the notch (~5,550 ft) between South Baring and the main (true) summit — this gully and basin hold snow late into the season, so an ice axe (and possibly crampons) are recommended into mid-summer; the step right at the notch is sometimes called the 'vertical snow wall,' and its difficulty varies year to year with snowpack. From the notch, scramble up and right a short distance, break out onto an open slope, then trend left/north across class 2-3 boulder and heather terrain toward the base of the summit block. Climb the summit block on its left (west) side via class 3-4 moves to reach the true 6,127 ft summit. A helmet is recommended from the boulder field onward given loose rock, and the whole outing is a long day (allow 8-12+ hours car-to-car).

set.beta: From the Church Lake trailhead at the end of FS Road 3160, an easy but steep unofficial path drops about 0.6 miles to Church Lake. From the lake the route continues around the shore and up through meadows toward a ridge/saddle above, then follows the ridge — which becomes steep but is 'nothing scary' — to a high point near peak 6066, with the final ~100 meters to the true summit requiring some class 3 scrambling on a narrow, occasionally exposed ridge. This is a hiker/scrambler route, not a roped climb; no technical gear is used on it.

The only documented ascent (Abegg's party, Aug 2012) climbed directly over the peak's east side and NW slopes rather than contouring around a subsidiary spur, finding mostly Class 3 terrain that is 'steep and mossy' with one or two unavoidable Class 4 moves; careful selection of moss and rock holds was needed on loose ground. Reported Day 1 stats for the full push from the road (including the Porkbelly Ridge approach and a descent to camp beyond the summit) were +6,550 ft / -1,820 ft over 6.3 miles — most of that gain occurs on the way to Berdeen's summit, with the loss coming afterward on the descent toward camp, so treat the raw numbers as slightly inclusive of travel past the summit rather than a pure car-to-summit figure.
set.approach: From the end of Bacon Creek Road (~850 ft, Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF), an intermittent boot path continues briefly along the old roadbed and the east-bank benches of Bacon Creek before angling up onto Porkbelly Ridge, the broad forested spur that climbs northeast toward Berdeen Peak. There is no maintained, numbered trail here — this is an unofficial climbers'-path/bushwhack route — and tread comes and goes through slide alder, vine maple, and devil's club in the lower timber, easing somewhat in open forest and heather bands higher up. Porkbelly Ridge is one of the brushiest approach ridges in this part of the range, so treat the brush-fighting and route-finding through it as the day's real crux, not the scrambling above. Bacon Creek, crossed or paralleled within the first mile or so above the road-end, is the last easy, reliable water; above that, plan on carrying water or relying on occasional seeps/lingering snow patches until you're near Berdeen Lake. The ridge gains steadily and steeply — roughly 6,550 ft of cumulative gain and 6.3 miles are logged for the full push from the road-end, over Berdeen Peak, and down to a camp above Berdeen Lake, which lines up with this route's on-file ~5,600 ft/23 km round-trip scale. Higher up, the ridge passes from brush into subalpine parkland and then rock/heather benches below Berdeen Peak's east side. One line contours around the summit on a spur ridge to avoid the top entirely, but most parties instead climb directly over the 6,400–6,420 ft summit via the east ridge/east side: easy-to-moderate terrain, mostly low Class 3 with occasional short Class 4 moves on steep, mossy rock, where holds need to be chosen carefully since moss-covered rock is slick, especially wet. Loose blocks and exposed dirt/heather steps along the ridge crest are the main scramble-specific hazards; a helmet is worth carrying. Near the summit, Berdeen Lake's turquoise basin opens up to the north/northwest. North-facing terrain along the approach ridge can hold lingering snow well into midsummer.

set.beta: First climbed as a six-pitch, Grade III 5.9 route by Alan Kearney with Jeff and Bill Thomas up the southeast buttress, following crack systems on the left side of a large slot high on the face over variable rock quality. The line has since been free-climbed harder and is now graded 5.11a with a well-protected finger-crack crux; it is now listed at 7-8 pitches, reflecting later variation starts (see 'Skinny Start').

set.overview: Big Kangaroo (8,326 ft) is the highest tower on Kangaroo Ridge, a jagged line of granite spires rising about two miles east of Washington Pass. This route — known as the West Face or West Route — is the original first-ascent line, climbed by Fred and Helmy Beckey with Walt Varney on June 21, 1942. It's a moderate Grade II outing: a steep gully approach up the west face followed by three short pitches of low-5th-class-to-5.6 climbing, finishing with an exposed, largely unprotected slab move to the small summit, guarded only by one old 1/4-inch bolt most parties don't trust.

set.beta: One of four named routes on Black Peak (alongside the South Route, Southwest Route, and Northeast Ridge). The lower section from Wing Lake is easy hiking/scrambling, transitioning into a gully system with a series of Class 3 and 4 steps described as 'fairly solid' rock. It sees far less traffic than the South Ridge or Northeast Ridge.

First ascended by Eric Wehrly and Sam Boyce in August 2023. Grade V, 5.10+, 16 pitches, with just over 2,000 ft of net elevation gain and about 2,800 ft of total climbing distance on the west face of the Southwest Summit (9,320'). The route sits 'looker's right' of its established neighbors, the Soviet and Oregonian routes. A weathered, decades-old cam found at pitch 4 suggests a prior abandoned attempt on similar terrain.

First ascended by Seth Keena and Erik Bonnett in early September 2013 (ascent dated 9/4/2013). Rated V, 5.9+, 2,200 ft total: 1,600 ft of new terrain (mostly sustained 5.6-5.8 with moves to 5.9+, via ramp/ledge systems) then 600 ft shared with the Soviet Route to the summit. It begins a few hundred yards left of the Soviet Route, making the Soviet and Oregonian the two established lines on this northwest wall. The first-ascent team's approach that year was an unusually long ~32-mile one-way trip (including ~10 miles of biking) due to ferry/road closures in effect at the time - this is not the standard approach.

set.overview: The original, easiest way up Pinto Rock's South Face — a moderate 4-pitch line up a gully/groove system on the west side of the buttress, listed as the 'regular' route.

set.approach: From the Ohanapecosh Campground day-use area (1,914 ft), follow the Silver Falls Loop Trail clockwise for about 1 mile; the boulder sits right off the trail and is hard to miss. As already noted on file, the Silver Falls Trailhead inside Ohanapecosh Campground is closed in 2026 for the Ohanapecosh reconstruction project, so this loop can't currently be started from the campground side — instead, approach via the Eastside Trail from the Grove of the Patriarchs parking lot, picking up the Silver Falls Loop from that end. This is an easy, well-maintained trail with essentially no gain or route-finding difficulty; Ohanapecosh/Silver Falls has running water nearby but none is needed for the short approach itself.

set.overview: Bryant Peak (5,801 ft) sits on the ridge between Chair Peak and The Tooth above the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, about 0.65 miles southeast of Chair Peak. Originally named Hemlock Peak, it was renamed in 1925 for Sidney V. Bryant; the peak was first climbed in 1926. It's a popular, moderate scramble often paired with Chair Peak and/or The Tooth on the Alpental skyline traverse. The standard line climbs a steep gully directly from Source Lake to the summit ridge.

Buck Mountain (8,534 ft) is the high point of the peaks ringing Buck Creek Pass in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, named for pioneer USFS surveyor Albert H. Sylvester. Its north and east faces are composed of dark, almost black schist that gives the summit a brooding look above the pass; the summit affords sweeping views of Glacier Peak (about 9 miles west), Clark Mountain (its taller parent peak, ~4 miles southwest), Liberty Cap, and Helmet Butte. First climbed in 1948 by Carl Suback and Ray Rigg, the peak is now one of the most popular scrambles in the area — typically climbed as a side trip from a multi-day backpack based at Buck Creek Pass, and rated as an Alpine Scramble.
set.approach: From the Trinity Trailhead (Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk) at the end of the Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 (~2,800 ft), follow Buck Creek Trail #1513. The trail splits from the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 within the first mile and climbs steadily through forest; around mile 2.75-3 it crosses the upper Chiwawa River on a footbridge that is weathered/damaged, so treat it with care in high runoff and have a wading backup plan in early season. Above the crossing the trail is a long, fairly shadeless, grinding ascent (mosquitoes/black flies are heavy in July) through forest and then subalpine meadow along the flank of Middle Ridge, opening into increasingly good wildflower and Glacier Peak views as you climb. At roughly 9.25-10 miles and about 3,000-3,300 ft of gain, the trail tops out at Buck Creek Pass (~5,800-5,900 ft) - one of the most scenic passes in the Cascades, with a reliable spring near the pass for water (last dependable source before the basin). Beyond the pass there is no maintained trail: pick up the well-used climbers'/boot path that switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap and the High Pass Trail junction, then leave that path to contour and traverse west/southwest, staying below Liberty Cap, into the upper basin below Buck Mountain's south and west aspects (Louis Creek Basin, ~6,700 ft) - the standard camp for a two-day trip. From the basin, ascend broad pumice and talus slopes and a low-angle snowfield (an ice axe, and crampons in early season, are worth carrying) to gain the south ridge around 7,400 ft. Follow the ridge crest through Class 2-3 terrain (stepping to locally 3-4 near a horn/gendarme close to the true summit) on loose, rubbly, slabby schist to the top; the summit crest has several bumps within feet of each other, so take care identifying the true high point. Primary approach hazards: rockfall/loose schist (helmet recommended, especially with parties above or below), the river crossing in high water, no reliable water source between the pass and the basin in a dry year, and route-finding above Buck Creek Pass since the climbers' path is intermittent. An alternate historic approach reaches Buck Mountain via Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa Valley, used for longer traverses.

set.overview: Bulls Tooth is a striking granite summit on the arcuate ridge rimming Chain and Doelle Lakes in the Chiwaukum Mountains, about 5.5 miles southeast of Stevens Pass in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness (Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest). It's one of the longest approaches out of Stevens Pass -- roughly 10 miles one-way via the PCT, Icicle Creek Trail, and the steep, unswitchbacked Chain Lakes Trail (#1569) -- rewarding backpackers with a quiet basin and a short, airy Class 3 scramble to a broad summit point. Note there is long-standing disagreement over which nearby point is 'the' Bulls Tooth: the name is mapped to a 6,807-ft triangulated point, applied to this higher 6,840+ ft high point (the one described in this route), and reserved by some locals for a lower, more fang-shaped 6,680+ ft summit near the Chain-Doelle pass that requires roped Class 4-5 climbing and a rappel. Runoff from the basin drains into Icicle Creek, a major tributary of the Wenatchee River.
set.approach: Start at the Stevens Pass PCT-South trailhead (large lot on the south side of US 2, ~4,060 ft, just east of the ski area buildings). Follow the Pacific Crest Trail south; the trail climbs gradually through forest and past Lake Susan Jane, staying high above Nason Creek before working into the Icicle Creek drainage. At roughly 4.5-5 miles from the trailhead, watch for the signed junction with the Icicle Creek Trail (leave the PCT here). Descend the Icicle Creek Trail about 2.6 miles, losing roughly 900 ft as it drops toward the head of the valley near Josephine Lake, to the junction with Chain Lakes Trail #1569. Turn onto Chain Lakes Trail and climb steeply — about 2.5 miles and 1,800-2,000 ft of gain through forest, brush, and talus benches — to the Middle/Upper Chain Lakes basin (~5,700 ft), the last reliable water and the standard base camp for the peak; tank up here, as there is no dependable water above the lakes. From camp, leave the maintained trail and go cross-country around the north/west shore of Upper Chain Lake, then ascend a talus- and scree-filled, northwest-facing couloir to Bullseye Pass (~6,200 ft), a broad notch on the ridge that serves as the staging area/gear cache for the final scramble — footing is loose here and rockfall onto parties below is a real hazard, so group up in the gully. From Bullseye Pass, contour and climb cross-country to the southeast on steep heather benches and white talus, gaining roughly 500-650 ft over about a mile below the tooth's northwest ridge to reach the base of the summit block. The final pitch to the top is Class 2-3 scrambling on solid granite; the easiest line works around the right (east/south) side of the summit block rather than the left, finishing with an exposed but short Class 3 step and mantle onto the summit. Beyond Chain Lakes the route is entirely unmarked cross-country travel, so route-finding competence, a map/GPX track, and comfort on loose talus and heather slopes are required; the upper mountain is fully exposed to afternoon thunderstorms with no bail-out shelter.

set.beta: Recorded in a single short first-ascent note by Don Williamson: 'Across the middle fork of the Snoqualmie River, two miles southeast of Big Snow Mountain lies P 6480, now officially Burnt Boot Peak. Bill Bucher, Tom Oas and I climbed a new route, the north ridge. From the base of the steepest part of the ridge, three leads of class five on granite, the last being a very sharp crest, led to easier ground. Three leads of class three and four put us on the summit.' The note records that the only previous ascent found in the summit register was that of a 1963 survey party (the peak's first ascent, via the easier scramble line). No repeat ascents of this line are recorded, suggesting it sees little to no modern traffic.

set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the short class 3–4 ridge step off the summit block back to the Point 5,841 pass, then descend the steep snow ramp below it facing in, plunge-stepping or self-belaying with an ice axe (a controlled glissade may be possible lower down if the snow is soft and the runout is clean and known — check before committing). From the base of the ramp, work back down through talus and boulders, staying climber's-right where possible to avoid the loosest scree, drop into the timber, and downclimb the brushy salmonberry/currant gully back to the cliff band. Pick a descending line through the boulder field to the river and re-ford to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no fixed rappel station or bolted anchor on this route, and the discipline (scrambling, not roped climbing) is consistent with that. In icy or wet conditions some parties might choose to build a single natural rappel (sling around a horn or tree) to protect the short class 4 step just above the pass, but that is a judgment call, not standard practice for the route. Note there is a separate, much harder roped North Ridge line on this peak (1971 first ascent by Williamson/Oas/Bucher, three leads of 5th-class granite) that is a distinct technical route from this scramble line and should not be confused with it.

set.beta: Ascends the gully dividing the west face, between the main summit rock and a false summit rock to the west. Starting north of Wings, follow a narrowing gully to a large chockstone, then climb around the chockstone to the NW notch of the summit. Described as 'fun in the winter, lots of loose rock in summer.'

This is one of the two main routes on Cannon Mountain and is 'only advised as an ascent route' -- most parties descend via the standard Prusik Pass/Druid Plateau line instead of reversing it. It's best done in mid-to-late summer once snow has melted from around Coney Lake and off the ridge. The route starts at the Eightmile Trailhead, climbs steep, bushy, loose burned slopes to the ridge crest, then follows and traverses below the crest -- including a notorious 0.3-mile loose traverse below a band of towers that can't be climbed directly -- before a talus gully and short final scramble to the summit block.
set.descent_text: From the summit, head to Prusik Pass and follow the standard route's trail through the Upper Enchantment Basin, down Aasgard Pass, and down the Mountaineer Creek/Colchuck Lake Trail back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. This is a demanding ~15-mile loop with sustained class 3 scrambling and bushwhacking on the ascent, requiring at least 12 hours car-to-car and an early start.

set.overview: Cardinal Peak (8,596 ft) is the highest summit in the Chelan Mountains, a remote subrange at the head of the Entiat River drainage, less than 5 miles from Lake Chelan. The peak has three summit points along its ridge; the standard route reaches the middle summit, traditionally treated as the highpoint, via a gully and ridge on the mountain's west side — though a June 2023 theodolite survey found the south summit is roughly 7 inches taller and is technically the true highpoint, reachable only via a short technical 5th-class scramble beyond the scope of this route. The north summit is a separate, harder Class 4 objective and is rarely climbed. Roughly 95% of climbers use the same North Fork Entiat approach, camping in the basin below Cardinal, Emerald, and Saska Peaks before a Class 3 scramble with real exposure near the top.

set.beta: Graded 5.8, the Northwest Chimney climbs three pitches of broken, loose rock - including an aesthetic but sparsely-protected chimney pitch - from the moat below the peak's northwest side to the summit. A 2013 party found the crux first pitch considerably harder than that grade (closer to 5.10) due to loose rock, and found no rappel anchors, pitons, or summit register, suggesting the route sees very few ascents.

This is the usual ascent line from the mountain's north side: traverse below the summit pyramid to reach the northeast ridge, crossing some steep gullies that hold snow, then follow the ridge crest to the summit with mostly class 3 and some class 4 moves. Total documented length is about 250 ft (76 m). The West Ridge is 'a more difficult and exposed' alternative by comparison.

A 5.7 trad route in The Castle's climbing area alongside the easy-5th-class Southeast Face; no detailed pitch-by-pitch description, approach specifics, or first-ascent history is on record. Likely approached the same way as the Southeast Face — via the Pinnacle Peak Trail from Reflection Lakes and a traverse across Pinnacle's south-face scree to the Castle-Pinnacle area.
set.overview: A three-star, low-fifth-class trad line in the small rock-climbing area on The Castle, distinct from (and reportedly higher quality than) the standard scramble/chimney route to the summit.
set.approach: Same as the Southeast Face: from Reflection Lakes (4,859 ft), take the Pinnacle Peak Trail 1.3 miles to the Pinnacle–Plummer saddle, then contour across Pinnacle's south-face scree/talus to the base of Castle's southeast side and scramble up broken ground to reach the base of the summit block.

set.beta: Also referred to as the West Ridge or the southwest slope, and universally described as the easy way up and the route of choice for descending after climbing the Southeast or North faces. From Upper Cathedral Lake (7,380 ft) take the trail 0.6 miles nearly to Cathedral Pass (7,600 ft), leave it, and climb easy sandy terrain for several hundred vertical feet. Ducks and cairns then lead over Class 2-3 granite outcrops, blocks and slabs — solid, coarsely crystalline rock with occasional spots where a friction hoist gets you over a block — to a hidden cleft running parallel to and just below the west ridge crest. There are two minor Class 3+ steps and one Class 4 step-across. The chasm that cleaves the summit rocks into north and south sections is the crux: step onto a large chockstone jammed in the slot and mantle onto a bulge on the far side. The climbing is easy; the exposure is dramatic, and most parties carry a rope and harnesses for it, often rigging a handline with prusiks for the return. In early season the chasm is filled with snow, which makes the first of the two step-acrosses easy or trivial; the second never has snow in the hole. It is Class 3 with exposure that makes it Class 4-.

The original Northeast Buttress is classified 5.7. A well-documented 2003 variation departs from the top of the original route's first pitch, heading left into loose class 4+ rock toward a left-facing corner with yellow-speckled rock and roofs above; pitch 3 climbs the crack system, traverses left under a roof, then continues on blocky climbing; upper pitches include a difficult 5.9+ left-leaning crack before moderate climbing to the summit. Overall grade III, 6 pitches, ~1,000 ft, crux rated 5.7/5.8 by the first-ascent party (route graded 5.9 overall).
set.overview: A longer, harder alpine rock line up Cathedral Rock's northeast side; a 2003 direct-start/finish variation to the original buttress line is a sustained 5.9, 6-pitch, Grade III climb.
set.approach: Approach as for the Cathedral Pass trail/Southwest Face route via Salmon la Sac and Forest Road 4330 to the Cathedral Rock trailhead, then to Cathedral Pass, from which the Northeast Buttress is reached.

set.beta: Put up by Mike Preiss and Mark Bunker in 2003. It starts where the original Northeast Ridge route ends its first pitch. From there, traverse left and up through scary, unstable Class 4+ rock on a short pitch, aiming for a left-hand vertical crack in a left-facing corner identified by yellow-speckled rock with roofs above. The crux third pitch follows that crack and exits over its left side — the route's best pitch, rated 5.7/5.8 and well protected. Above, the rock eases and parties navigate upward through variations, with a short difficult left-leaning crack at 5.9+ before moderate terrain leads to the summit area. It carries a PG13 protection rating and would deserve a higher star rating were it not for the precarious second pitch.
set.approach: Drive to the Cathedral Rock trailhead (Trail #1345, ~3,350 ft) via I-90 Exit 80, SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald about 14.8 miles, then 12.3 miles of gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 and the NF-153 spur. Sign the free wilderness permit at the register. Hike trail #1345 past Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake, ~4,850 ft) at 2.5 miles to the Cathedral Pass / PCT junction at 5,550 ft, 4 miles in. From there the northeast side is reached the same way as the Northeast Buttress: cut across the meadow to the stand of trees (a good gear cache), then traverse under the east face across talus toward the northeast side of the peak. Note that this route begins from the top of the original Northeast Ridge route's first pitch.

set.beta: Documented as a class 5.6 route on the peak's southeast side; no further pitch-by-pitch beta is available.

Documented only informally — no page with pitch-by-pitch beta was found. The line begins on Chair's north ridge and follows the crest toward Bryant on 4th-class to low-5th-class rock, with one short, steep mandatory rappel (~50 ft) getting off Bryant — the same rappel found on the closely related 'Tooth - Chair Traverse,' which covers the Bryant-to-Chair portion of this ridge system.

Rated 5.2 (PG13) over 3 pitches, 600 ft (182 m); about 400 ft of the route's pleasant climbing is 4th to easy 5th class, with the notable overhanging band rated 5.5. Protection is sparse in places, with runouts over 50 ft reported on the traverse pitch.

From the basin below Chair Peak's East Face, the route climbs a curving gully system on climber's right before trending up and left along the buttress crest to the summit. The technical crux in winter conditions is a short, steep ice bulge encountered partway up; in summer the route is straightforward exposed scrambling with occasional low-5th-class moves. It is commonly done in 4 pitches with a 60m rope, though many parties simul-climb sections or break it into 5-6 shorter pitches, especially in early-season snow. Short approach and moderate climbing make it very popular and prone to queues on clear winter weekends.

This is a 6-pitch, 1,000 ft (303 m), Grade II, 5.7 trad route reached via the East Face approach to 'Thumbtack Rock' before angling right over the ridge. It has a low average rating (2/5 stars) reflecting run-out climbing and poor rock quality in places.

The summit can be reached either by hiking the Chelan Butte Trail from a WDFW trailhead on the south side of the town of Chelan (via Iowa Ave, roughly 7.46 mi round trip with 2,500 ft gain) or by driving/walking Chelan Butte Road from the Millard St trailhead in the Lakeside community (4.5 mi one-way, paved for the first 1.2 mi then dirt/gravel). Both converge on the same summit-road system. A bench at the Elephant Head viewpoint offers a rest stop partway up. The route is fully exposed to sun with essentially no shade.

Established in 1989, this is the second-best-documented line on Chianti's east face and a quieter alternative to Rebel Yell at a full grade easier. It starts "directly below the summit," following "a long left-leaning ramp up into a left-facing corner and an off-width crack," then "three more pitches led up, crossing Rebel Yell, and finally gained the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti. A short pitch led to the summit up the normal route." Approach and descent logistics are identical to Rebel Yell - the same Early Winters Creek trail to Burgundy Col, the same drop and traverse beneath Burgundy Spire's east face, and a rappel-based descent. It is listed as "Lichen Bouquet, II 5.9"; the same east-face line is elsewhere graded III 5.9. Published beta is thin: pitch lengths and a total footage are nowhere given, so this is a route for a party comfortable route-finding on an alpine face rather than following a topo.

set.overview: Chimney Peak (6,917 ft, correcting the older 6,913 ft figure) is a rugged, remote summit in the central Olympics on the west side of the Mount Anderson massif (parent peak West Peak, 7,365 ft, 3.4 mi NE). It sits immediately north above Enchanted Valley, the "Valley of Ten Thousand Waterfalls," with over 4,800 ft of relief rising from the valley floor in less than a mile. The peak's name comes from "The Chimney," a 100-ft rock tower on its west aspect first climbed (5.3) by Mike Banner and Vern Johnson in 1970; the mountain was originally called "Old Snowback" and its summit was first reached in 1941 by Tolvo J. Nelson. The standard ascent follows the southwest ridge on Class 3-4 terrain with loose rock and real exposure near the top.
set.approach: From the Graves Creek Trailhead in the SW corner of Olympic National Park, follow the East Fork Quinault River Trail (Enchanted Valley Trail) east. The first roughly 2 miles follow an old roadbed through big firs and cedar before a short, steep drop to river level; at 2.5 miles the trail crosses Pony Bridge, a narrow, photogenic span over a fern-lined gorge — a reliable early water source before the long valley slog. From there the trail undulates through old-growth rainforest (spruce, alder, maple) to O'Neil Creek Camp at about mile 6.7, then crosses No Name Creek and Pyrites Creek around miles 8–9.5 (Pyrites has camps on both banks, ~12 sites total, and is a good staging point for a two-day approach). Beyond Pyrites the trail climbs gently for several more miles, including a high bridge roughly 20 ft above the river that can feel exposed if snow-covered early season. Around mile 13 the trail opens into Enchanted Valley (~2,000 ft) at the historic chalet, directly beneath Chimney Peak's southeast face, which rears 4,800 ft above the valley floor in under a mile — far too steep and cliff-bound for the standard route. From the valley (climbers appear to peel off the maintained trail somewhat short of the chalet, roughly mid-valley), leave the trail and work cross-country around the mountain's south/southwest flank — brushy, unmarked, boulder-and-timber route-finding with no cairns — up a drainage that gains the SW ridge crest, where the Class 3 scrambling begins. Given the 13-mile one-way trail approach, most parties camp in the valley (Pyrites Creek or Enchanted Valley) and climb the peak as a long day from camp rather than car-to-car.

From US 101 about 36 miles north of Hoquiam (one mile south of Amanda Park), turn east on the Lake Quinault South Shore Road and follow it toward the head of the valley; the first ~10 miles are paved and the remainder is gravel, ending after roughly 20 miles at the Graves Creek Trailhead (47.57255, -123.56997, 550 ft). Note the current detour: Olympic National Park lists South Shore Road closed at mile 8 for a washout, with Graves Creek Road reachable via the North Shore Road instead — check park road conditions or the road hotline at 360-565-3131 before you drive, and note that RVs and trailers are prohibited on Graves Creek Road. From the trailhead, follow the East Fork Quinault River (Enchanted Valley) Trail up the rainforest valley. It is 27.8 miles round trip and about 3,700 ft of gain to Enchanted Valley, so roughly 13.9 miles and a high point near 2,035 ft one way; the Enchanted Valley Chalet (47.67528, -123.38917) sits at about 2,000 ft directly beneath the peak's south wall. Chimney Peak's south side above the valley is a 4,800 ft wall of cliffs and waterfalls and is not the way up — the climbing approach leaves the trail and works around to the peak's southwest side to gain the Southwest Ridge, then traverses to the base of The Chimney on the west aspect. The off-trail line is nowhere published in detail. The gainFt figure above is the sum of two figures (~3,700 ft of trail gain plus ~4,900 ft from the 2,000 ft valley floor to the 6,917 ft summit) rather than a measured track.

set.beta: No detailed move-by-move description of this route has been written down; it is on record as sharing its start with Caravan, which breaks right after the 3rd bolt — Chitlins is presumed to continue more directly.

set.overview: Cloudy Peak (7,915 ft) rises directly above Cloudy Pass at the head of the Lyman Lakes basin in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, part of the Cloudy Pass batholith (~20-million-year-old intrusive rock). It's a popular add-on for parties doing the Spider Gap-Lyman Lakes loop or the longer Buck Creek Pass/Suiattle Pass circuit, with summit views of Glacier Peak, Bonanza Peak, Chiwawa Mountain, Dumbbell Mountain, and the Lyman Lakes/Lyman Glacier basin below. A Mountaineers party made the first recorded ascent in 1921. Most of the route is an easy talus/heather walk-up, but the true summit is a short, exposed rock spire that pushes the route to Class 3-4 — don't mistake the easy approach for the whole picture.

A scenic, non-technical approach/scramble route to the col between Colchuck Balanced Rock and Colchuck Peak, used both as an approach for the harder rock routes and as a moderate objective in its own right. The line is rated 3rd class overall (Grade II).

Columbia Peak (7,172 ft) is a sharp, glacially-carved summit in the Monte Cristo group of the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, forming a cirque with neighboring Monte Cristo Peak and Kyes Peak (its line parent) that holds the Columbia Glacier and the popular, turquoise Blanca Lake below. The standard route — the West Spur, rated Grade I, Class 3-4 — is reached via the historic Monte Cristo ghost-town approach out of Barlow Pass: typically a long single day or, more commonly, an overnight camp at Twin Lakes, followed by an off-trail ridge traverse and a varied, blocky scramble with one exposed 4th-class move around 6,700-6,800 ft.

set.beta: First climbed the same day as the peak's other documented technical line (July 31, 1963), by a separate Mountaineers rope of four who 'climbed directly up the east face from the glacier (class 3-4),' during that season's Northern Pickets climbs. No later account describing a repeat of this specific line was found; modern parties have used the northwest-couloir/north-ridge line instead.

set.overview: The South Buttress is the classic long moderate alpine route on Cutthroat Peak, a wandering 12-pitch line (16 by a finer pitch breakdown) up the road-visible south face with a memorable chockstone crawl, a stembox crux, and a splitter offwidth on the summit ridge.

set.beta: First climbed by Andy Cairns and Bryan Burdo (Affiliated Climbers of the Montlake Erratic). The route climbs the northern cirque via a central chimney system — possibly a melted-out variant of an earlier 1974 Kloke-Simon line — for four pitches, then exits left onto an exposed rib for three pitches of delicate face climbing, before re-entering a gully with large ('monstrous') chockstones leading to the summit. Part of the first ascent was done by moonlight.

Almost all the difficulty here is brush, steepness and route-finding rather than climbing. The rock is rated Class 4, but that grade comes from a climber who climbed it in January and has been honest about the limits of that experience — he can only guess at the difficulty of the rock and the number of pitches, if any, because good snow may have covered the harder steps.

From the Gorge Creek bridge at 1,096 ft the slope is sustained from the first step, gaining roughly 1,800 ft in the first half mile through small evergreens with a salal and brush understory. There is no trail, and numerous rock outcrops make navigation important. One recorded line: from near the highway curve, hike due north to about 2,800 ft, turn northeast and ascend to the 4,920+ ft point, then go straight uphill on a bearing of about 340 degrees true to Point 5872, where the south ridge becomes obvious. A party approaching via Gorge Creek instead took the South Buttress, turning cliff bands at about 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft on the right, moving through open timber and alpine snowfields, and reaching the South Davis saddle at 5,700 ft in 4.4 hours from the car; they described Class 2-3 scrambling on the buttress with slime-coated rock slabs near the top. A third account has the granite slabs starting around 4,850 ft after a brushy gully at 3,600 ft, bypassing Point 5872 to the north, and reaching a south-ridge viewpoint at 6,300 ft.

From the 5,720+ ft saddle, the instruction is to 'climb 200 ft of slab to the sharp ridge leading to the summit.' In good snow this is step-kicking; bare it is class 4 slab. In snow this is where the route's steepest ground is — the notch on the old standard south ridge line is reported at 65 degrees, which is precisely why skiers pushed a variation onto the southwest face. Above it the crest broadens into an almost level, wide-open ridge to the summit, one of the great walkable viewpoints in the range and simultaneously the top of the largest cornices most people will ever stand near. In summer that broad snow crest may instead be a scramble among rocks with steep drops on both sides.

There is also a variation that its climber did not rate: from the saddle, drop east into the basin under the east side of the south ridge, traverse up and north as far as possible, then turn west and climb beside the cliff edge. The turn involves a ten-foot step that looked trivial and was not — iced-in cracks and wrong-feeling holds, passed with ice-axe belays. His verdict on the direct ridge, descended on the return, was that it 'had all the ledges we needed to get down'. Take the ridge.
set.descent_text:
Descend the south ridge crest directly rather than reversing the east-basin variation. The step that drops into the saddle looks formidably steep from camp — steep enough that at least one party detoured around it on the way up — but it is climbed down easily, with all the ledges you need. Below the saddle, retrace your line through Point 5872 and the open slopes.

The work is in the forest. Stay on the line you came up: the cliff bands near 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft need to be turned on the correct side, and getting them wrong means rappelling off trees. Slabs low on the mountain are covered in slippery moss, and one party reported a 3rd-class chimney with an awkward move below it as the crux of the descent. Expect deadfall fields. Total descent time is about 4.1 hours from the summit for a fit party moving well, and every account calls it brutal on the knees.

If you are descending this route after climbing the northeast face, the strong advice from the party that did it is to get the top 1,500 ft done in daylight — that is what lets you avoid the cliff bands — and to carry a compass, because the timber is dense enough to hide the dam lights and a drift to the north puts you back in Stetattle Creek.

There is almost no descent-specific beta for Der Dihedral beyond the note that it 'joins the 1972 NE Arete to finish.' Since the route tops out on the same upper mountain terrain as Backbone Ridge, the standard descent is the same walk-off used for that route and for the summit generally: scramble/snow traverse southeast to a saddle, then east across the long snow slope to Aasgard Pass, and down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) to Colchuck Lake, favoring climbers' left near the granite walls. Crampons/axe are worth carrying into mid-summer. A rappel alternative exists on Backbone Ridge's finish for icy conditions (ledges below the summit to a rap station, two rappels to a ledge system, then a scramble north to Aasgard Pass) - if Der Dihedral's top-out lands near that same station it may be usable, but this has not been confirmed for this route, so plan on the standard walk-off by default.

set.beta: 1,100 ft, Grade III, nine pitches. The route is listed at 5.11- (2 stars); the original first-ascent account describes it as 5.10, Grade III. Details beyond length, pitch count, and first-ascent party are sparse.

set.descent_text: Because every route converges on the same small summit and the whole formation is only ~200 ft tall, descent is by downclimbing rather than rappelling. Reversing the low-angle North Ridge scramble on the west/north side is the easiest way off if you didn't come up that way; there are no bolted or fixed rappel stations on the formation.

set.overview: A 7-pitch, 5.10- granite rock climb up Dome Peak's South Face, established as a new route around September 2, 2011 — a rarely-repeated alternative to the standard Dome Glacier route for parties seeking real rock climbing on the peak.

set.approach: No route-specific trailhead or approach beta for this boulder problem turned up anywhere online, and the name itself reads like a locally-known or in-joke label rather than a catalogued, widely-documented line — it isn't cross-referenced anywhere against a named boulder or trailhead in the Glacier Peak area. Based on the on-file numbers (0 pitches, no elevation gain listed, and a roughly 1 km/0.6-mile approach distance), this is a short, low-commitment boulder problem reached by a brief, mostly flat walk from a pullout or trailhead rather than a sustained mountain approach. Expect an informal boot-path or use-trail through forest/talus for under a mile with negligible elevation change; watch for the usual approach hazards of the Glacier Peak Wilderness at low elevation — wet roots and mossy rock in the trail tread, and blowdown after storms — but nothing resembling glacier travel, creek fording, or avalanche terrain given the minimal distance and zero gain on file.

set.descent_text: Parties who top out into the upper Triple Couloirs exit typically continue, unroped, down the standard boot-packed couloir/gully system used to descend Triple Couloirs, then continue to Aasgard Pass and descend its snow slope (glissading is common) back to Colchuck Lake - one documented winter ascent finished exactly this way, unroped after the couloir and glissading most of Aasgard Pass. This is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel descent, on every ascent on record. Crampons and an axe are standard for the whole descent; both the couloir exit and Aasgard Pass carry avalanche, rockfall, and icefall hazard, so timing (early starts, stable snowpack) matters more than technical descent gear. No rappels are recorded for a completed ascent, though a party that gets high on the face but cannot continue over the top could face a difficult retreat down steep ice/mixed terrain that might require an improvised v-thread or gear rappel - this is not recorded anywhere but is a reasonable contingency to plan for on a Grade IV ice/mixed route.

From the top of the couloir/Pandora's Box, descend left and traverse northeast to the true summit (some parties rope up for this exposed traverse), or alternatively exit about 30 ft below the notch, scramble Class 4 rock roughly 20 ft, and follow the ridge left to the top. From the summit, the standard descent is southeast to a saddle, then east across a long snow slope to Aasgard Pass, then down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) to Colchuck Lake - stay climbers' left near the granite walls and beware drifting climbers' right into cliffs near Colchuck Peak. Crampons/axe are recommended into mid-summer; early season the descent can largely be glissaded. No rappels are needed on this standard summit-and-Aasgard-Pass finish. If a party instead retreats directly back down the couloir rather than topping out, downclimbing steep snow/ice or building an improvised rappel off natural gear (slung chockstones or horns) in the couloir could become necessary - this specific scenario is not recorded anywhere but is a reasonable contingency to plan for on a technical, mixed alpine couloir.

set.beta: Fully bolted 5.10b/c sport pitch on Sofa King Buttress, positioned as the leftmost route on the wall. The line (FA party Wylie Moreshead) is known for the sheer variety of technique packed into one pitch rather than a single hard crux — 3D stemming, backstepping, flagging, a roof, laybacking, jugs, crimps and underclings. Protected by 12 bolts to chain anchors at the top; photos of the route show the crux section and a rest stance before an upper bulge.

This is agreed to be the peak's easiest line and it involves scrambling rather than roped climbing; no guidebook-level pitch-by-pitch or mileage description could be located despite an extensive search.

set.overview: A less-traveled line up Witches Tower's east/southeast aspect, climbing broken, blocky Class 4 terrain; only a handful of ascents are on record (it is logged as a 4th-class rock route that's occasionally graded up to Ice 2/Mixed 1b, reflecting a short snow or low-angle ice step that can persist on the upper face into early summer).

set.beta: The East Ridge begins with a bergschrund crossing and several pitches (mostly 5.7, often simul-climbed) up vegetated ledges and blocky rock to gain the ridge crest and east face. A 5.8 pitch leads into the route's signature crux: a sustained hand/fist crack (5.9) that nearly every trip report singles out. Above the crux, moderate 4th/low-5th-class climbing continues along an exposed, knife-edged crest to the true summit. The route is graded III, 6 pitches, 800 ft, but many parties describe the full outing — including simul-climbed sections — as feeling more like 8-10 pitches / Grade IV given the long glacier approach and multi-rappel descent.
set.overview: Widely regarded as one of the best rock routes in the Picket Range and among Fred Beckey's favorite North American climbs. First climbed by Fred Beckey, Dave Collins, and Ed Cooper in October 1958 (weekend of Oct 5), on a second attempt at the then-unclimbed east ridge. The route starts at the base of the south face, gains a col to reach the ridge proper, then follows about 8-10 pitches of mid-5th to 5.9 climbing on sustained, exposed, excellent rock, highlighted by a 30m sustained 5.9 hand-and-fist crack and an airy final low-5th traverse across the summit ridge to the top.

The East Slope (East Ridge from Lucky Pass) is Primus Peak's standard, easiest line — Class 2-3 rock and moderate glacier travel above a long backcountry approach up Thunder Creek. It's the most commonly described route on the peak, often combined with neighboring Tricouni Peak (8,102 ft) from the same col.
set.approach: Start at the Thunder Creek Trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20 (turn in just past milepost 130). Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly 6-6.7 miles to McAllister Camp, then continue past Tricouni Camp (~8 mi) and leave the maintained trail to climb the climbers' path up 'Lucky Ridge' to a bivy near the northeast corner of the lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier (~6,000 ft). One detailed trip log (Aug. 2018) recorded 8.25 miles and 4,760 ft of gain from trailhead to this camp in about 9 hours. Note: the trail bridge over Thunder Creek near McAllister Camp has been reported washed out in past years, requiring a log crossing or wade — check current NPS trail-conditions postings before you go.

set.overview: Elephant Head (~7,990-7,995 ft) sits at the northwest end of a series of jagged crags extending about 1.1 miles off Dome Peak's twin summits in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, dividing the Dana Glacier (west) from the Chickamin Glacier (east). Its summit cliffs plunge into the ice-sculpted cirque at the head of Agnes Creek's West Fork. Unlike Dome Peak itself, Elephant Head has almost no independently documented route history - it is essentially always climbed, when climbed at all, as a side trip from a Dome Peak high camp or during the Ptarmigan Traverse, sharing the same long approach and glacier crossing.

set.beta: This is the generic 'easiest route' taken by nearly every party that visits Emerald Peak, almost always as a side-summit from a basin camp shared with Cardinal and/or Saska Peak. It is described consistently as: gain a basin around 6,800-6,900 ft below the Cardinal-Emerald saddle, cross talus/scree to the base of a broad gully, climb the gully (moderate snow early season, loose scree/rock later) to a notch in the summit ridge, then turn and scramble class 2-3 rock (described as short — 'a very short class 3 scramble near the top') to the summit. This line has no formal name; 'Southeast Ridge' describes the ridge/notch it gains relative to Cardinal Peak, which sits just SE of Emerald.

Despite the peak's craggy appearance suggesting no easy line exists, erosion has cut a class 3 gully/weakness up the west side that is catalogued as a named, rated route (skill 2 / fitness 2). It tops out on a summit divided into two high points roughly 100 ft apart — the north summit is slightly higher, and the south summit has notably more exposure, with a steep slab dropping toward the East Face. Access is via the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 from the standard trailhead, or alternately via the Emerald Park Trail #1230 starting from Lucerne on Lake Chelan's shore (a boat-access approach).
set.overview: A distinct, dedicated line on the peak: an easy class 3 scramble to Emerald's twin summit block via an erosion-carved gully on the peak's west side, reached from the same North Fork Entiat trailhead (or alternately from Lake Chelan via the Emerald Park Trail).

set.approach: From Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry (or a floatplane) to Stehekin Landing. Ride the NPS shuttle bus 4.4 miles up Stehekin Valley Road to Harlequin Bridge ($5 fare), cross the bridge, and follow the road past Harlequin Camp and the Stehekin Airport to pick up the Stehekin River Trail. Follow this mostly flat trail southeastward about 3 miles to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction. The Devore Creek Trail then climbs steeply through rock bluffs and open forest for about 1 mile, enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, and traverses brushy, dry hillside for roughly 3 more miles to Bird Creek Camp (4,200 ft) — the only designated camp in the area, with room for about three tents. From Bird Creek Camp, most parties do Flora as a long day round trip: bushwhack through open forest (spiderwebs, chest-high brush, and blowdown reported) toward the saddle south of Enigma Peak, then follow the route description above to the summit.

set.beta: From a horn near the summit, make the first of five single-rope rappels (roughly 400 ft total) down the northeast side to a series of ledges. Follow the ledges east - mostly 3rd class with short 4th-class moves at rib crossings - across roughly five rock ribs, staying well below the ridge crest, then a short gully leads back up to the ridge crest near the solitary gendarme on the East Ridge. Cairns mark the easiest line across most rib crossings (a higher and lower cairn at each rib), and parties consistently report finding them.

Also known as the "Chiwawa River route," this line is frequently combined with an ascent of neighboring Chiwawa Mountain from the same high camp at the ~7,200 ft col. Rock quality is notably better on the East Ridge itself than in the approach gully or on Fortress's southwest face.

Very little beta exists online for this line beyond a single forum report: it follows the left side of the visible northeast face, with steeper rock and snow options further right of uncertain quality/rock condition. Expect a mixed rock-and-snow outing rather than a simple scramble, with a rope needed for the pitched rock section. One climber who used it noted that the published descriptions of it are inaccurate.

set.overview: A short, fun friction slab climb up the center rib of a distinct slab left of the crag's original JMK-established routes; first put on record in 2023.

This is the standard glacier line up Little Tahoma, named for the two glaciers it crosses (Fryingpan and Whitman) rather than for the east-shoulder terrain feature; modern route guides describe "Fryingpan/Whitman Glaciers" and "East Shoulder" as the same standard route — same Summerland approach, same Whitman Notch crossing, same Class 3-4 summit block — first climbed August 29, 1894 by J.B. Flett and Henry H. Garrison. See the East Shoulder route entry on this peak for the closely related (likely identical) line.

set.approach: From I-90 Exit 34 (North Bend), drive Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (FR-56) east — paved at first, then good gravel — staying on FR-56 past the Taylor River Road (FR-5620) junction to a wide gravel wash / old borrow-pit pullout on the north side of the road near the base of the mountain (trailhead elevation roughly 1,150-1,200 ft). There is no maintained, numbered Forest Service trail here — this is an unmaintained climbers' boot path marked intermittently with cairns and pink flagging tape, not a hiking trail. From the wash, follow the dry creekbed/streambed uphill for roughly a mile; a boot path exits climber's-left into second-growth forest with light brush before the creek narrows. Multiple boot-path branches exist low down — avoid the flat, early traverse that cuts to the slab too low, and instead take the higher, up-and-down traverse. Around 2,200 ft the path enters a loose dirt-and-scree gully mixed with vegetation (unpleasant, roughly 400 ft of gain), then exits climber's-left onto a wooded ridge for another 400 ft of steep but relatively brush-free hiking. At about 2,900 ft you reach the base of the first major slab; parties solo (or rope up, depending on comfort) two low-5th-class pitches following intersecting dikes, then continue up dirt/heather above the slab's upper-left edge. Above the slab, route-finding gets serious: intermittent boot path, cairns, and flagging lead through a 'tiny notch,' a knife-edge 'razorback,' and a flat bivy site known as the 'glade saddle' where many parties break the day with a bivouac. A short wooded ramp with one sporty 20-ft scramble step follows, then a rope-up point at an exposed ledge traverse leading to the 'Y Notch,' where the route joins the gully system locally called '#2 Gully' — loose rock on one side, polished/mossy rock on the other — for the final roughly 600 ft of short technical pitches to the summit ridge and high point (5,519 ft). Total gain is about 4,400 ft over roughly 1.5 miles one-way from the wash; budget 5-7+ hours up in good conditions. There is no reliable water past the initial creek near the trailhead, so fill up early, and only attempt this route bone dry — the slabs and dirt gullies become treacherous when wet.

set.beta: The old sketch landmarks are still the way people navigate it: dirt gully, slab, canyon edge, tiny notch, razorback, glade saddle, key ledge traverse, Y notch, #2 gully. Walk up the dry creek bed from the road; partway up the route leaves the streambed into the woods on faint trail and flagging. At about 2,200 ft you reach the dirt gully — fill water at the creek here, it is the last certain water on the route. Four hundred vertical feet of loose dirt and rock, then the trail exits left into brush-free timber for another 400 ft, then the slab, which is two pitches of comfortable soloing on intersecting dikes. Above the slab continue in dirt along its upper left edge, traverse under a rock outcrop, over the razorback and tiny notch to the Glade Saddle, where there is a tight, well-used two-person bivy site. The wooded ramp above has a sporty 20-foot step. The Key Ledge Traverse is the most overstated part of the description — after the dirt gully it feels like a walk. It ends at the Y Notch, the confluence of #1 and #2 Gullies at the head of the Great Canyon. A short exposed step around a rock band, then several hundred yards of very steep brush and brush-tunnel on faint trail, brings you to the base of #2 Gully. The gully is a nightmarish mix of impossibly loose rock on one side and polished mossy rock on the other — do not attempt it unless bone dry. Simulclimb the lower section with short belayed steps, then pitch out the harder ground; a fixed ring piton partway up may date to the 1940 first ascent. The 'Chimney Variation' (two leads of easy class 5 above the chimney, a good idea if the chimney is wet) rejoins the standard line at the top of #2 Gully around 5,200 ft, from where easy slabs and steep heather lead to the summit.

Ghost Peak is normally climbed as an add-on from a high camp shared with neighboring Crooked Thumb Peak and Phantom Peak, since all three summits are within a few tenths of a mile of one another in the Northern Pickets. Access from camp is 'obvious' once you're established there. The first-ascent party's own account: 'The route was from the notch south of the peak which was gained from the west. We stayed on the south and west sides of the mountain following obvious weaknesses' — easy-to-moderate 4th/low-5th-class climbing on comparatively solid Pickets rock.

Catalogued as a distinct technical alpine route from the southwest standard route, but very little published trip-report detail exists — the north and east faces of Golden Horn are noted regionally as sheer and infrequently climbed.

set.descent_text: West Face tops out on Guye's south summit (where the route tops out and the register sits; GPS surveys suggest the north summit may be marginally higher) at ~5,169-5,172 ft alongside the middle and north summits, and the descent is a scramble/rappel traverse north along the connecting ridge rather than a reversal of the climbing line. From the south summit, follow the climber's path around the east (right) side of the middle summit to the notch between the south and middle summits. The drop into the gully here is loose, mossy class 3/4 slab; most parties rappel rather than downclimb it. The total rappelling on this route comes to roughly 100 ft, enough that many groups get by with an arm-wrap/hip rappel off a sling rather than a full rap setup, though bringing a rope and device is still the sane default. Important: there is a tree at the top of the gully between the south and middle summits that climbers should specifically NOT rappel from (flagged as unsound/inadvisable in route notes) — use the established sling/anchor lower or to the side instead. Past the middle-summit notch, descend the gully and slabs to the right (east side) to go around the north summit, then scramble up an easy gully to the notch on the north summit's north side. From there, a well-defined scrambler's trail leads down past a small pond, then west (left) back to the Alpental parking lot. Bring a single 30m+ rope and rap device even though the raps are short — anchor tat and rock quality are inconsistent year to year, and the loose gully rock is a real hazard for parties above/below each other. Expect 1 rappel as the norm on this route (occasionally a short second one depending on exact line through the middle/north notch), well short of full pitch length.

set.overview: The north side of Guye Peak is reached via the separate Cave Ridge Trail rather than the West Face talus approach, and is best known as the 'North Route' — a class 3-4 scramble to the north summit that is also run as a scrambling-course objective, not a sustained roped rock climb. A short optional 'Hidden Ridge' variation near the north/middle notch adds one 5.4 move protected by a single ~30 ft rappel off a slung horn. This is measurably easier, and approached differently, than the 5.6-5.8 technical rib route on Guye Peak; the class 3-4 scramble description is consistent across accounts.

set.beta: Half Moon is a SW-to-NE trending rock fin on Kangaroo Ridge between Wallaby Peak and Big Kangaroo, with solid, steep, crack-laden faces. Documented lines include the 1942 first-ascent (original) route, rated roughly Class 5+ (low 5th class) — the easiest known way to the summit — plus at least one modern route, Uncle Wehrly's Toupee (5.10-, trad), and at least 3 other difficult unnamed technical lines. None of these is a non-technical scramble.
set.overview: Half Moon is a crescent-shaped granite fin on the north half of Kangaroo Ridge, between Wallaby Peak (0.23 mi south, the peak's higher neighbor) and Big Kangaroo (8,326 ft) to the north. It sits about two miles east of, and in clear view from, the North Cascades Highway at Washington Pass. The rock is ~45-million-year-old rapakivi-textured granite of the Golden Horn batholith. Fred and Helmy Beckey, with Walt Varney, made the first ascent on June 17, 1942. There is no easy walk-up: at least three technical lines are known (Southwest Ridge, North Ridge, South Face), all involving sustained Class 3-4 scrambling with at least one low-5th-class move. This entry covers the Southwest Ridge, generally regarded as the least difficult option, which finishes with a short, low-exposure Class 4 step just below the summit.

set.beta: Helmet Butte is normally climbed as part of a Buck Creek Pass backpacking trip rather than a car-to-car day climb, given the ~17.6-mile round-trip approach. From a point at 5,600 ft on the Buck Creek Pass Trail ('Waypoint 86'), the recommended line turns off-trail toward Pass No Pass on a well-defined but braiding boot path, gains a notch around 7,200 ft below the summit block, then finishes with a short, low-exposure Class 3 scramble on solid rock, aiming for the block's south (left) side for the easiest line. An alternate line continues past the trail junction to Buck Creek Pass itself, then climbs steep grass and heather slopes to the west side of the summit block before the same short scramble - this option is likely hazardous when wet.

set.overview: Hibox Mountain (6,548 ft) is the high point of Box Ridge, a rugged sub-ridge of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness about 5 miles east of Snoqualmie Pass, rising above the popular Rachel Lake basin. It's one of the most-climbed scrambles near I-90, combining an easy trail approach with a steep, loose Class 2-3 boot path up Box Ridge and a short, exposed Class 3 summit block. Summit views take in Rampart Ridge, Alta Mountain, Three Queens, Mount Thompson, Rachel Lake, and the Stuart Range.

set.beta: P1 climbs past bolts to chains at roughly 5.10+. P2 moves right and up a slab reported as '5.12? — not freed as of 2015', i.e. the pitch's grade and completion status are unresolved in the available beta.

set.overview: Hozomeen Mountain is a dramatic, dark twin-summited peak rising directly from the east shore of Ross Lake near the Canadian border in North Cascades National Park/Ross Lake National Recreation Area. The higher North Peak (~8,071-8,072 ft) and slightly lower South Peak (8,003 ft) are built of Hozomeen chert, a hard but badly fractured bedded rock that gives the mountain its dark color and its reputation for notoriously loose, rotten climbing. The South Peak's nearly 1,000-foot near-vertical face (average angle ~42.6°) is often cited as the steepest in Washington. First ascents: North Peak, Sept 6 1904 (Sledge Tatum & George Loudon Jr., via the northeast); South Peak, May 30 1947 by Fred Beckey and five companions via the Southwest Route. The Southeast/South Face line described here is regarded as the least committing of the three known lines to the South Peak's summit, in contrast to the harder Southeast Buttress (Grade III, 5.6, FA 1988 by Adams/Goodman/Johnson/Petroske) and North Face (IV+ 5.9, FA 2019 by Rolf Larson & partner).
A two-pitch moderate line up the right side of Huckleberry's south face, possibly corresponding to a vaguely described 'south face' route on the peak.

set.beta: From Hannegan Pass, parties gain Ruth Mountain (via its glacier/snow slopes), then descend Ruth's south ridge — 'talus and slabs below a rock ridge' with casual 2nd-3rd class climbing on generally good rock — to the Ruth-Icy Saddle, from which Icy Peak is clearly visible. From the saddle, crampon up firm snow toward the notch between Icy's Northwest and Southeast summits, then climb the Southeast Peak's Northwest Ridge — reported as 'steep, loose, wildly exposed' — to a Class 4 knife-edge summit ridge leading to the true (Southeast) summit, finishing with a 100-ft 4th-class summit gully.

The lower northeast ridge section climbs 4th-to-easy-fifth-class (5.4 max) slabs and cracks on excellent rock.
