It's followed by the crux upper east-face pitch, graded 5.6 X on rock described as horrible, with almost no protection - this 'is not a good route for the average 5.6 climber' and choosing the wrong line on the face 'could have fatal consequences.' A 70 m rope and a light alpine rack are needed.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the ridge and the Class 2–3 gully back down to the North/South col, then pick your way back down the talus, slabs, and any lingering snow to Lake Ingalls, and rejoin Ingalls Way Trail #1390 back over Ingalls Pass to the Esmeralda Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble — no fixed rappel anchors exist on the standard South Peak route and the great majority of parties downclimb the entire route car-to-car in a day. Watch for loose rock and scree in the gully below the col (parties should stay bunched or descend one at a time to avoid knocking rock onto climbers below), and for the same lingering steep snow/ice near the col noted on the approach, which can make the downclimb more consequential than the ascent, especially early or late season. Some parties in icy conditions choose to sling a natural rock horn or block near the col and back up the short Class 3 step with a hand line or short rappel for extra security, but this is a personal-judgment call, not a standard part of the route, and no such anchor is left in place.

set.beta: Documentation of this line is sparse, and there is no full route description. Climbers who have scouted it describe very poor rock overall — 'as bad as anything in the Olympics' near the summit ridge — with a possible band of somewhat better rock on the north side, but caution that any existing description should be taken 'with a grain of salt' and the line ground-truthed in person.
set.approach: Drive to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (Trail #833.2) in Olympic National Forest: from US 101 near Sequim Bay State Park turn onto Louella Road, continue about a mile to Palo Alto Road and turn left for roughly 1.1 miles to the forest boundary, where Palo Alto becomes Forest Service Road 28. Turn right on FS 2880, pass Dungeness Forks Campground, then stay left on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles to the trailhead just across the Dungeness River bridge (47.877572, -123.136927). There is a large parking area and a vault toilet but no potable water; a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required. Hike Upper Dungeness Trail #833 up the river — an easy, shaded, river-grade trail past good swimming holes — reaching Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Camp / Boulder Shelter at roughly 6.1-6.4 miles (~4,890 ft). Continue on the Constance Pass trail as it climbs out of the timber into rocky, flowery terrain beneath Warrior Peak and Inner Constance, crossing into Olympic National Park, and drop to Home Lake at about 9.3 miles (~5,308-5,330 ft, ~500 ft below Constance Pass). Put simply, the approach is 8.5 miles up to a base camp near Home Lake. From the lake, work up the Home Creek basin south-southwest toward the peak and camp at the large boulders directly northwest of the summit, just south of Home Creek; the face is in full view from there and from below, which is the only reliable chance you get to pick out the ramp and the green-lichen ledge.
set.descent_text: There is no maintained or fixed descent on this face. Because the route finishes with low-angle terrain, most of the upper mountain can be reversed on foot with care; the steeper buttress below the Class 3/4 gully is where you will need to rappel, and every station has to be built and abandoned since there is no fixed gear on the route. Carry cord, tat and spare nuts specifically for this. Rappelling loose Olympic basalt is its own hazard: pull ropes deliberately, keep the party out of the fall line, and expect the ropes to knock blocks off on every pull. Once back at the boulder camp, retrace the Home Creek basin to Home Lake and reverse the Constance Pass / Upper Dungeness trail to the car. Note that the walk out regains meaningful elevation over Constance Pass before the long descent to the Dungeness, so budget more time for the exit than a simple downhill mileage estimate suggests.

set.overview: Inner Constance (7,672 ft by LiDAR) is the fifth-highest summit in the Olympic Mountains, a rugged pyramid just west of Mount Constance (its line parent, 0.9 mi east) across the glacially carved Avalanche Canyon, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. The mountain is built of Eocene tilted pillow basalt, rotten and loose throughout. David Harrah's party is credited with the first ascent in 1939. The commonly described standard line climbs out of Avalanche Canyon via a South Gully/snow-filled defile to the East Ridge ('Route 2A') rather than via nearby Crystal Pass, which is a separate saddle/viewpoint climbers sometimes visit instead when they bail on the summit. Climbers occasionally report uncertainty about whether they've reached the true high point versus a nearby sub-summit in the Olympics' notorious cloud cover.
set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the class 3–4 blocky terrain back down the rising traverse to the step above Crystal Pass. Route-specific rappel counts for this exact Crystal Pass/NE line are thinly documented, but the Constance massif's upper terrain that Inner Constance shares with its neighbor — broken, gendarmed ridge steps on notoriously poor rock — is commonly down-climbed by confident parties with one short rappel used through the single steepest step near the top by those who prefer it. Plan on roughly one rappel of about 30 m/100 ft; a single 30 m rope (or a 60 m doubled) is enough length. Treat any anchor as natural rather than fixed: the only documented technical route on this peak explicitly notes 'no fixed gear' and 'very poor rock, very poor pro,' so expect to sling a horn/block or build a hand-placed gear anchor and inspect (or replace) any tat you find rather than trust it blindly. Below that step, continue down the same broken class 2–3 ground back to Crystal Pass, then reverse the approach: down into Crystal Basin, over Constance Pass, and back down the Constance Pass Trail and Dosewallips Road to the washout trailhead. Loose rock and scree are a hazard the entire way off the summit block — this is classic crumbly Olympic metavolcanic rock — so keep parties tight and out of each other's fall line. There is no easier walk-off alternative; the class 4/low 5th step near the top is the only way through, whether downclimbed or rappelled.

set.beta: One of Jack Mountain's established routes.
set.approach: No single approach is established as standard. The record of the Skoog ascents places the start low on the glacier on the east side of the mountain, so the route is gained from the glaciated eastern flank rather than from the Jerry Lakes side. Practical access to that side is either from the Canyon Creek Trailhead (~1,900 ft, SR 20 near MP 141) via the McMillan Park-Jackita Ridge Trail #738 and cross-country travel around the mountain's southeast side, or from the Ross Lake East Bank Trail on the west and north. Both are multi-day propositions; most parties on Jack take three to four days for any route. Because no turn-by-turn approach exists for the East Ridge, study satellite imagery and earlier trip accounts before committing to a line.

set.beta: This is an early-season snow climb, done when the north cirque is still filled in. From the East Bank Trailhead follow the East Bank Trail roughly 8 miles to the May Creek camp, then leave the trail and climb about 3 miles of steep, bushy, cliff-banded forest — cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are passed on game trails — to reach snowline near 4,800-5,000 ft and a camp either on the flats around 5,200 ft below the glacier or higher on the glacier itself around 7,400 ft. The Nohokomeen Glacier runs from about 6,100 ft to 8,200 ft, is over 340 acres, and is heavily crevassed after the midpoint of its descent, so rope up. Above the glacier the headwall is the crux: it is variously described as 700 vertical feet of snow at slopes up to 60 degrees, and as a sustained 50-55 degrees for about 800 feet with steeper steps. Most parties simul-climb it, taking turns kicking steps, with a rope over the shoulder for the bergschrund; winter parties have pitched it out with pickets, cams, nuts and screws through a mixed cliff band. The bergschrund is the main obstacle and normally goes on a single bridge on the left side. Above, exit onto the ridge and finish along a narrow, corniced summit ridge with rocky drops — the last few hundred feet are the most exposed of the route.
set.overview: The classic north-side snow route on Jack Mountain and by far the best documented line on the peak: the East Bank Trail to May Creek, a steep bushwhack to the Nohokomeen Glacier, then roughly 2,100 ft of crevassed glacier and a 700-800 ft headwall of sustained 50-60 degree snow to a corniced summit ridge. The round trip is rated at 30 miles and 10,000 ft of gain and graded an intermediate alpine climb.

set.beta: One of Jack Mountain's established routes.
One of Jack Mountain's established routes; no grade has been recorded for this line.

One of Jack Mountain's roughly seven established lines, nearly all class 4. A class-4 'Southeast route' and a 'South Face' are recorded separately, distinct from a harder, direct 5.6/Grade III 'Southeast Ridge' first climbed in 1977 — see Corrections below for how this DB entry likely maps onto those.
Listed separately from the mountain's standard class-4 lines as a Grade III, 5.6 climb.
One of Jack Mountain's established routes; no first-ascent party or date has been recorded for it.
set.approach: Park at the Panther Creek / East Bank trailhead on SR 20 near milepost 138 (~1,800 ft), 18.5 miles east of Newhalem. Follow the East Bank Trail 2.4 miles west to a multi-way junction, then take the rightmost branch — the old Little Jack Trail, built by the Forest Service in the early 1900s for pack-animal grazing on the mountain's meadows. This climbs steadily to Little Jack at 6.0 miles from the car, gaining roughly 4,800 ft from the junction to the 6,745 ft summit. From Little Jack, continue north along the ridge crest to the notch, then traverse across to the base of Jack Mountain proper and the start of the southwest ridge. Water is scarce on the ridge - plan on carrying or on the meadows' seasonal sources. This is the shortest way to the peak, but the Little Jack traverse takes real stamina.

From the parking pullout on spur 270, an unmarked climbers' path ascends directly up the boulder field on the hillside toward Tyler Peak Crags; there is no formal trailhead sign. The Full Montey sits on the upper bench of the Tyler Peak crag system, reached by climbing up past the base of the adjacent Mossness wall/sector to gain the upper bench. Because the approach trail is unofficial and unsigned, most parties rely on a written area description or GPS beta rather than a marked trail; expect a steep, brushy bushwhack-and-boulder-hop of a few hundred vertical feet from the road.

set.beta: From a high camp in the basin below Mesahchie Peak, climbers side-hill traverse west along Kimtah's south face at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft, crossing more than a dozen loose ribs and gullies (mostly class 3). A well-known 'red ledge' cuts across the ribs and greatly simplifies the route-finding. Near the 'Grotesque Gendarmes,' the standard line downclimbs about 150 ft down a buttress and threads a narrow, exposed class 4 gully to bypass a cliff band, then regains the traverse. A final broad, solid-granite gully (class 3) leads up to the ridge just west of the true summit, finishing with a short class 3 scramble across a scree saddle between the west and east (true, 8,649 ft) summits.

set.overview: Kololo Peaks is a sprawling, multi-summit massif on the southern flank of the Glacier Peak (DaKobed) massif, about 3 miles south of Glacier Peak itself. It has been called 'almost a nunatak' because it is nearly surrounded by ice - the White Chuck and Suiattle Glaciers flank it to the west/north and the Honeycomb and White River Glaciers to the east/south. It's a Class 2-3 snow/glacier objective, not technically hard, but the combination of a 12+ mile approach (much of it off-trail), extensive glacier travel, and remote route-finding make it a serious undertaking reserved for parties with solid glacier-travel and navigation skills.

set.beta: The route's crux is packed into the first ten feet: a technical, pumpy opening sequence that has caused many climbers to fall low. Once past this tricky start, the remaining climbing to the anchor is comparatively reasonable. Photos of the line show technical hooking/mixed-tool sequences, indicating it is regularly dry-tooled as well as rock-climbed.

set.overview: Let it Burn closely parallels the popular West Face, sharing its approach and first pitch before splitting left up a fairly obvious, sustained thin-crack system. Established by Jens Holsten and Max Hasson at grade IV 5.12a, the crux is a sustained 130-foot 5.12a pitch featuring technical face moves connecting crack systems via 'wild knobs.'

The Lewis Creek Route is the original 1915 first-ascent line up Gunn Peak, named for the Lewis Creek drainage the FA party used on their approach. It is rated 3rd Class (3 stars) and its modern access is via overgrown logging roads leading to a climbers' trail beginning around 3,200 ft on the ragged, brushy crest north of Barclay Creek — essentially the same corridor used by today's standard (Southeast/Tailgunner Pass) approach. It is climbed far less often than the standard line today and is largely of historical interest; expect an unmaintained, easy-to-lose path.

set.approach: Park at the Smithbrook Trailhead (elev. ~3,800 ft) on Smithbrook Road (FR 6700), about 2.7 miles up from Hwy 2. Start on the signed Smithbrook Trail (part of the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness trail system) and climb via nearly 20 short switchbacks, gaining about 650 ft in 1.2 miles to Union Gap on the PCT — Lichtenberg's summit is visible to the south for much of this stretch once the forest opens up. At Union Gap, turn left (south) onto the Pacific Crest Trail and follow it about 2 miles, contouring below Lichtenberg's east flank, to Lake Valhalla (~4,830 ft), passing through a mix of forest and open meadow/heather and crossing Smith Brook along the way (a reliable water source and a good place to filter before leaving the trail). From the north or east shore of Lake Valhalla, leave the PCT and begin the off-trail portion: contour and rising-traverse around the lake toward the peak's south/southwest side, picking through heather benches, boulder fields, and increasingly loose talus. There is no maintained trail above the lake — expect real route-finding, some bushwhacking through scattered subalpine fir, and a few short cliff bands that force minor backtracking; a GPS track or written beta is genuinely useful here. The standard line aims for a prominent gully on the south/southwest side of the summit tower (often snow-filled into early summer — an ice axe and sometimes light traction are worth carrying outside of peak summer), climbed as scree/talus with a bit of low third-class scrambling near the top to gain the final summit block. Total gain from the trailhead is roughly 2,000-2,500 ft over about 7 miles round trip, with 6-7 hours being a typical leisurely round-trip time.

set.beta: This is the line described as a ridge that 'just screams skin me in winter'. In summer it is a 7-mile, 2,100-foot scramble starting from the first switchback on Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 and following the Lichtenwasser Lake fishing trail to a saddle on the southeast ridge. Jim Brisbine's party climbed it as a rock scramble over 20-21 September 1975, camping at Lichtenwasser Lake and continuing over the true summit to The Lichtenhorn before descending the west ridge. The winter version has you leave the road at the first major hairpin, head southwest up wooded and steep but always snowshoeable hillside, traverse toward Lichtenwasser Lake at about 4,600 ft (crossing the lake if it is frozen), then take easy slopes to the ridge crest and follow the summit ridge to the top. A winter north-side version is given with compass bearings: ski 2.6 miles up Smithbrook Road, leave it before the major switchback near 3,970 ft, follow a true bearing of 177 degrees to Lichtenwasser Lake, then 248 degrees from the lake's south end to a 5,640-foot saddle, and ascend the southeast ridge to the summit — about 5.2-plus miles, rated 2 to 2+ in skill and 2-minus in fitness, and included among the classic backcountry ski and snowboard routes in Washington. Avalanche hazard is the defining concern; both sides of the mountain present it.

A January 2002 ascent recorded as 'Lichtenberg Mountain West Face 5.9+' was made by James Nakagami, climbing with Dan 'Danimal' Capellini and a third partner. The wall sits just above Lake Valhalla; the approach is a short walk from the Smithbrook trailhead of about an hour, and it is an easier walk in than Snow Creek Wall — the implicit pitch for the crag. A 'grand west face' is separately listed as one of the mountain's three distinct routes, and a party is on record as having been turned around by the sheer wall before eventually reaching the summit by an easier line, which corroborates that this is genuine roped terrain rather than a scramble. Beyond the grade, the location and the approach, the beta is thin: no topo, pitch count, rack list or descent description is available. Treat this entry as a pointer to a real but poorly documented line, not as a route description. Anyone going should expect to do their own reconnaissance from Lake Valhalla, and plan for a full trad rack and a walk-off.
set.overview: A roped rock line on the steep west wall that rises directly above Lake Valhalla — the feature known as Lichtenberg's 'grand west face' and the reason parties who try to scramble the peak from this side get turned around by the sheer wall. Reported at 5.9+ and reached in about an hour on foot from the Smithbrook trailhead.

set.approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as the standard line: start at the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (FS Road 39, Trail #677) near Glacier, WA, and follow the Heliotrope Ridge Trail roughly 2.7-3 miles through old-growth forest and several avalanche-chute creek crossings to the flat former Kulshan Cabin site (~3,200 ft), the usual camp/staging area. From there, climb the Hogsback moraine to the toe of the Coleman Glacier and rope up for glacier travel — but where the standard route cuts southwest toward the Thunder Glacier cirque, the north ridge/north-face approach stays higher and further climber's-right (east) on the Coleman Glacier, traversing beneath the Coleman icefall to reach the north-facing cirque wedged between Colfax Peak and Lincoln Peak. This is a longer, more exposed glacier traverse than the standard approach: you pass directly beneath active serac bands on the Coleman Glacier's upper icefall for a stretch, so icefall/serac collapse is a real objective hazard here and timing (early morning, before the glacier softens) matters more than on the SW-side approach. The line aims for the base of Lincoln's roughly 1,000-ft north face/ridge, a route first climbed in May 1958 (Cooper and O'Conner) that 'demanded ice screws' — meaning it's genuinely an ice/mixed objective, not a snow scramble, and conditions (rime, verglas, bare ice) vary a lot by season and year; go early-season (spring) for the best ice, which also generally means better-bridged crevasses on the glacier crossing.

set.beta: The route climbs the gully/face system above a col south of the peak. Parties approach via Ingalls Creek and Crystal Creek to a tarn/col at roughly 7,700-7,880 ft, then scramble ~100 ft of easy Class 3 talus before roping up for two full 60m pitches of low-5th-class granite (a crack/slab pitch, then a rightward traverse into a chimney), finishing with a short Class 3 section through boulders to the summit plateau. One notable hazard is a ~20-ft unprotectable 5.6 slab section below the approach col with no crack systems for gear.

This is a rarely climbed, route-finding-intensive scramble rather than a well-trodden trail. A 2014 party (Jim Brisbine) climbing from a camp at Williams Lake found the crux to be a wildly exposed notch on the northeast ridge, then Class 4-5 moves on a steep southwest face near the true summit; the party descended the 'easier' Class 3 east face but still ran into cliff bands that forced a traverse back onto the ascent line. A separate account similarly describes exposed Class 3 moves on the east face and a short Class 3 section gaining the north ridge, and a short rock notch is noted that some parties rate as low fifth class.

Ascend steep snow from the center of the Green Creek Glacier and cross a potentially tricky moat/bergschrund to gain the center or right side of the 500-ft-wide face. Climb sustained, moderate 5.4 face climbing on solid rock for roughly 600 ft (4 pitches), then continue over easier, looser terrain — the full wall, including this upper scrambling, is nearly 1,000 ft top to bottom.

This line was skied as part of a multi-day (May 12-14) south-to-north ski traverse of the Twin Sisters Range by Chris Simmons, Mark Allen, Greg Balco, and Paul Kimbrough. The traverse's technical crux involved roughly 40 m of 4th-class rock followed by 100+ m of 50-degree ice and mixed terrain, with the descent of Little Sister's South Couloir singled out as the trip's best line; the descent required 100+ meters of rappelling, including a fixed final rappel with a knot pass.
set.overview: A steep snow/ice/mixed couloir on Little Sister's south side, called out in a 2007 account of the first known ski traverse of the entire Twin Sisters Range as 'the proudest line of the trip.'
set.approach: From the Elbow Lake Trailhead on Forest Road 38 (Middle Fork Nooksack Road), the Elbow Lake Trail reaches the Middle Fork Nooksack River within a few minutes. THE BRIDGE IS GONE and has been for decades — the Forest Service states plainly that there is no bridge over the river to reach the north trailhead and that fording may not be possible during high flows. Parties cross on whatever log is currently in place. One group used a log crossing roughly 200 yards east of the trail junction; another used an unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing. Assume you will have to hunt for it, and treat the crossing as the crux of the day in terms of consequence. Once across, follow the Elbow Lake Trail — reported in remarkably good shape — through old-growth for about 1.5 miles. Just before a sharp switchback (near Hildebrand Creek), find the blazed Green Creek climbers' path branching off and heading up the Green Creek drainage. It is marked with small blue diamond trail markers. Follow it past the Wiseman Lake outlet at about 2,850 ft, then up through the brush-filled Green Creek valley, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier. The Green Glacier approach is 5 miles one way with 4,000 ft of gain from the trailhead over trail, climbers' trail, boulder fields, scree and slabs. For the South Couloir specifically, continue up the basin and climb snow to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of Little Sister, then traverse onto the south side and up into the gully. In deep winter one party found hard snow all the way to the col; snowshoes were left at the snow line and crampons carried from there.
set.descent_text: Descended (not climbed) as part of the range traverse using 100+ meters of rappelling, including a fixed final rappel requiring a knot pass.

set.beta: The standard line climbs scree, talus, and broken ledges on Luahna's east/south-facing slopes to gain the south ridge, then follows the ridge crest toward the summit. It is described as a 2nd-class line, but most parties encounter a short Class 3-3+ traverse or step to bypass a gap in the ridge below the true summit. The route is glacier-free but crosses persistent snow and loose rock well into summer, and is commonly combined with adjacent Clark Mountain in a single long day or overnight trip.

Recorded in Sept 2000: approach from the White River Trailhead via Boulder Creek, over a sheepherder's trail through Boulder, Clark, Luahna and Chalangin basins, to a high camp near 5,800 ft below Luahna. The summit push climbs class 2 ledges on the south face onto the ridge, crosses an exposed class 3+ traverse on the north side beneath the summit, then finishes with class 3 scrambling straight up to the top.

Parties reach the east end of the Terror Glacier via the same Terror Basin approach as the West Ridge, then climb roughly six pitches of alpine rock (up to 5.8-, rated PG13) up the southwest ridge/face to the summit. Pitch-level detail is not recorded here; most parties climb it fully roped rather than scrambled.

set.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the route itself, back down the same line you climbed — do not try to walk off. Eight single-strand rappels, all off bolted, fixed anchors (this is a sport-bolted line, so no natural gear or v-threads needed): rap 1 from the P7/summit anchor down to the anchor at the base of pitch 7; rap 2 face-rappels to an anchor set left and above the dihedral; rap 3 is a short drop to a ledge-side anchor beside the dihedral; rap 4 goes to one of two anchors at the pitch 4 stance (favor the left one); rap 5 is a short, free-hanging rap off an upper-P3 anchor aimed at a ~10 ft tree left of the line, with an intermediate anchor in a nook below it; rap 6 is a vertical face rappel down lower P3 to a large ledge at the pitch 2 anchors; rap 7 drops to the pitch 1 anchor (10–15 ft left of the original belay); rap 8 finishes at the base. A single 70m rope is sufficient for all 8 raps; two 60m ropes also work if you'd rather split gear or prefer doubled-rope security, and some parties carry a single 60m instead but report tighter/more numerous transitions. Because you rappel the entire route back to the start, many parties leave approach shoes and packs stashed at the base. Descent hazards: loose rock sitting on several of the belay ledges (manage ropes and stack carefully to avoid kicking debris onto the party below), some rope-stretch/rope-snag potential given the zigzagging (not straight-down) line of anchors, and lingering steep snow in the approach gully in spring that can complicate the walk back to the Sunrise Mine Trail after the last rappel.

Descend by reversing the final scramble pitches/downclimbing back to the top of the technical face (the on-file 'downclimb/scramble to the top of the East Face' is accurate for the uppermost section), then begin a rappel sequence rather than trying to downclimb the buttress itself — the rock is loose enough that down-climbing the route is not recommended. From a small ledge/anchor on the east side just below the summit, a 50 m rappel gets you down the steepest upper wall (rockfall-prone — the next rappeller should move off to the side immediately, not straight down, to avoid anyone above). Below that, parties generally find 2-3 more rappel stations working down toward the notch system: a single 60 m rappel to a belay/anchor stance, followed by an overhanging section that's typically rappelled on doubled rope (i.e., a full 60 m rope folded, giving ~28-30 m of rappel) down to just below (north side of) Gunsight Notch/the V-notch. Accounts are not fully consistent on the exact count — some describe essentially 3 key rappels down this line, others log 4, and one description notes '5 rappels will get you down... a 60 m rope is long enough' — the variance reflects rope length used and which anchors parties link together. Plan on 4-5 rappels with a single 60 m rope (or 2x 30 m/60 m doubled) to be safe, and treat 3 as an optimistic minimum if you're able to link stations with a full 60 m strand. Anchors are natural/fixed, not bolted: expect slung trees, horns, and boulders with aging webbing/cord — inspect every anchor before weighting it, back it up if it looks tired, and carry a knife and spare cord/webbing since parties have had to replace or rebuild anchors mid-descent. The first station below the staircase is reportedly in a tree at the top of the drop overlooking the V-notch. Once down to the notch, reverse the snow/scree gully and the traverse back across Mixup's east flank to Cascade Pass and out the trail to the trailhead; if you camped at Cache Col/Kool-Aid Lake, break camp there instead of continuing all the way to the car. Watch for rockfall from parties above throughout the descent, and be alert for a moated-out Cache Col in late season if that's part of your exit.

set.overview: Monte Cristo Peak (7,136 ft) is the technical centerpiece of the Monte Cristo Group, a tight cluster of peaks (Kyes, Cadet, Columbia, Del Campo) ringing the ghost town of Monte Cristo in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. Unlike its neighbors, Monte Cristo has no scramble-only line to the true summit: the standard and most-climbed route, the North Col Route, requires roped 5.6 rock climbing through a short chimney above the col, so it's properly a Basic Alpine Climb rather than a Class 3 scramble. The peak was first climbed in 1923 by James M. Keyes and W. Zerum, and was described in 1918 as 'a huge pile of red rock.'

Morning Star Peak (6,020 ft) sits above Headlee Pass and the Sunrise Mine basin between Sperry and Del Campo Peaks, in the Mountain Loop Highway corridor of the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District). The standard route follows the Sunrise Mine Trail to Headlee Pass, then leaves the trail for a Class 2-3 talus-and-heather scramble up the peak's south/southwest slopes to the summit ridge. The South Ridge scramble is rated T5/S4 — a 'rugged, beautiful and challenging true scramble' requiring comfort on steep rock and snow — tougher than the Class 2-3 label alone suggests, especially in early season. Route-finding above Headlee Pass takes some care; cairns thin out and the terrain funnels through steep heather benches to the summit block.

set.approach: From the Barlow Pass gate, walk the closed road (old railroad grade) approximately 4 miles to the Monte Cristo townsite; a backcountry campground sits at that mark. Mossy Loaf's coordinates place it essentially at/immediately adjacent to the townsite itself, so once at the flat of Monte Cristo the formation is only a short distance further off the main townsite path. The exact final spur to the specific wall is not well established, so on-site scouting is recommended for the last stretch.
set.descent_text: From the top of the route, downclimb the easy slab above the crux or scramble off along the wall's edge back to road level. The standard walk-off between tiers involves some bushwhacking, which is one reason the neighboring route You Moss Be Joking exists as a lower-impact link.

set.beta: From the Austin Pass/Lake Ann trailhead, hike the maintained Lake Ann Trail, which drops roughly 900 ft into the Lake Ann basin before climbing back out. Near the Lake Ann junction, leave the trail and work up heather benches and talus, staying fairly high on the east side of Mount Annette (nicknamed 'Little Ann') rather than dropping into brush, then continue up a gully (often snow-filled and roughly following a fault line) to gain the summit ridge and the top of Mount Ann. The off-trail portion is generally straightforward Class 2 route-finding, though boot paths can peter out higher up and steeper sections may warrant an ice-axe self-belay. Reported round-trip stats vary by GPS track/route taken (10.5 mi RT / 4,000 ft gain is the commonly listed figure; individual logs have recorded figures as low as ~11 mi / ~3,400 ft), reflecting that this is an off-trail line rather than a fixed path.
set.approach: From the Austin Pass/Artist Point trailhead (paved lot at the end of SR 542, roughly 58 miles / 1.5-2 hr from Bellingham), follow the signed Lake Ann Trail #600, which drops about 700 ft into the Swift Creek headwaters basin before climbing back up past Lake Ann (4.1 miles one-way to the lake area) to a 4,900-ft saddle northwest of the lake. From the saddle, leave the maintained trail for a boot path heading southwest then south along the ridge crest; where the ridge steepens near 5,300 ft the path contours the east side before the crest re-forms — follow cairns over Peak 5681 and scramble roughly 0.5 mile west along the summit ridge to Mount Ann. Total round trip is about 10.5 miles with roughly 4,000 ft of cumulative elevation gain.

set.overview: Cockscomb Ridge is the true north ridge of Mount Baker — a long, prominent rock-and-ice ridge forming a skyline on the north side of the peak, distinct from the popular 'North Ridge' route (which is actually the NW spur). It sits between the North Ridge and the Park Glacier Headwall and is approached from the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead across the Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers. First climbed in its entirety on July 4, 1961 by Chuck Murley, John Musser, and a third climber, after a 1906 Mazama party had been turned back by the ridge's 300-ft Cockscomb Tower.

set.approach: Start from the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (~3,700 ft, reached via Glacier Creek Rd 39 — note the road washout adds ~9 mi/2,000 ft of extra approach on foot/bike before you even reach the sign-in kiosk). Trail 677 climbs through old-growth forest and flower-filled avalanche chutes; watch for a couple of unbridged creek crossings that can be awkward early season or after rain. At roughly 2.25 mi the maintained trail forks — the left fork continues to the Coleman Glacier overlook, the right fork is the climbers' path that drops toward the moraine and begins the real work. Past Kulshan Cabin's former site (~4,800–5,000 ft, last reliable running water before camp), the trail climbs steeply up the crest of the lateral moraine known as the Hogsback. Most parties establish high camp somewhere on or near the Hogsback between about 6,500 and 7,200 ft — either on the ridge itself or on the flat benches toward the Black Buttes/Roman Nose — roughly 3–3.5 mi and ~3,000 ft above the trailhead. Above camp there is no water except what you melt. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and cross the broken lower Coleman Glacier: the line generally trends up toward ~8,000 ft to meet the North Ridge tracks before dropping back down and cutting under the Roman Nose to reach the base of the headwall near 8,500 ft. This glacier crossing is a genuine route-finding crux that changes year to year — it can involve weaving around large crevasses, crossing questionable snow bridges, and occasionally a committing, barely-reversible crevasse jump or a short vertical step to get established at the base. Because the headwall and the Black Buttes shed rock and ice as the day warms, most parties leave camp in the pre-dawn hours (11 p.m.–4:30 a.m. starts are typical) specifically to be on or past the exposed glacier crossing and lower headwall before the sun hits it.

set.beta: Mount Berge's premier technical route: nearly 2,000 vertical feet of generally low-angle, low-to-mid 5th class granite ridge climbing broken by a distinct notch and a burly 5.8 chimney crux, finishing through a series of towers and gendarmes to the summit. It is commonly graded III, 5.8; a detailed 2019 account grades it IV, 5.8, describing consistently solid rock allowing fast simul-climbing except at the crux.

set.approach: Drive to the Crater Creek Trailhead (4,750 ft, 48.2205 / -120.26801). From Twisp take SR 20 south 2 miles to the SR 153 junction, then SR 153 south about 12 miles to County Road 1029 and on to CR 1034 (Gold Creek Road). CR 1034 becomes Forest Road 4340 after roughly 5 miles; continue about 1.6 miles further on FR 4340, then turn onto FR 4340-300 (Crater Creek Road) and follow it 4.6 miles to the trailhead. An alternate description of the same drive starts from Carlton: south on SR 153 for 3.5 miles, right on Gold Creek Loop Road 1.6 miles, right on Gold Creek Road 5.0 miles (becomes FR 4340), 1.6 miles more, then left on FR 4340-300 for 4.4 miles. The gravel is washboarded in places — drive it slowly. From the trailhead take Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The first 0.7 mile climbs gently, rounds a bend into an opening with a view up the Eagle Creek valley, then descends slightly to the bridge over Crater Creek. From there the trail climbs at a consistently gentle grade through mature pine into subalpine fir and larch. At roughly 5 miles the trail reaches the Eagle Lakes area and forks: take the RIGHT fork toward Upper Eagle Lake (7,115 ft, 48.213553 / -120.346815, about 5.9 trail miles and 2,350–2,430 ft of gain from the car). Upper Eagle Lake has many campsites and a large horse camp, and is the last reliable water. From the lake, the East Face of Bigelow is the wall directly above to the northwest — bear northwest up talus and heather to the base of the golden granite, roughly 0.4–0.5 mile and 900–1,000 ft above the lake. The FA party logged the whole thing as '8 miles more or less from TH, ~3500' to base' and called it a great, fast trail. Scout the line from the lake and from the base before racking up; the crack systems are genuinely hard to read from below.

set.beta: The standard (and only non-technical) line on Buckindy climbs class 4 terrain on the north slopes, close by glacier remnants on the mountain's north and east flanks. There is no maintained trail to the peak itself — parties reach it via a multi-day, largely cross-country ridge traverse, most commonly starting from the Green Mountain Trailhead to the south via Suiattle River Road, or alternatively via the Kindy Ridge climbers' trail off Cascade River Road to the north, following the connecting ridgeline of the Buckindy Range. Separate class 5 rock climbing exists on the southwest-facing 'Buckindy Crags,' outside the scope of this standard scramble route.

set.overview: Mount Carrie is the highest point of the Bailey Range and the scenic centerpiece of the classic Bailey Range Traverse. Despite this route's name, there is no trail or known route connecting Hurricane Ridge to Cat Basin or Mount Carrie — Hurricane Ridge sits on the opposite (east) side of the park and is used only as a distant viewpoint of Carrie's glaciated north face. Every recorded ascent instead approaches from the Sol Duc River Road trailhead on the park's north side, via Heart Lake, High Divide, the exposed "Catwalk" ridge crossing, and Boston Charlie's Camp/Cat Basin, before gaining Carrie's southwest ridge and a broad south-facing scree basin to the summit.

set.approach: Two standard approaches leave from the Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) area near Slate Peak (~6,900-7,400 ft, one of the highest drivable roads in Washington): (1) the shortest line drops from Slate Pass/Buckskin Ridge down the West/Middle Fork Pasayten River to Fred's Lake/Fred's Pass, then crosses upper Eureka Creek toward Shellrock Basin below the Carru-Lago-Osceola cirque — about 15 miles one-way; (2) the Monument Creek Trail, also off Harts Pass Road, is roughly 19 miles one-way with more up-and-down elevation change. From a Shellrock Basin or Eureka Creek camp, gain the Carru-Osceola col or Rolo Pass and scramble the south/southeast talus slopes to the summit ridge. Pasayten trails are lightly maintained — expect blowdown on the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail and stretches where the tread is fainter than GPS basemaps suggest, so off-trail navigation skill is required.

set.beta: A distinct line from the standard West Route. It has been described as 'basically an alpine scramble with two pitches of harder climbing on the steepest part of the ridge,' but a recorded attempt found the ridge heavily coated in moss and heather, making the two technical pitches far slower and harder than the nominal grade suggests.

Classified a 'Basic Alpine' climb, roughly 10 miles round trip with about 4,600 ft of elevation gain from the historic Grade Creek Road trailhead; a detailed account of a camp-based west-ridge/northwest-face variation logged 14 miles and 6,400 ft round trip. The crux is not technical difficulty but the arduous, often overgrown approach; the final few hundred feet to the summit involve a steep snow ramp/gully flanked by rock bands, commonly climbed with an ice axe and crampons in early-to-mid season.

A 2012 account of down-climbing this ridge from Crowder's summit toward Pickell Pass describes it as: 'a convoluted path of grassy 3rd class ledges' with an occasional 4th class move and 'one or two short 5th class downclimbing moves... pretty tedious and definitely don't-slip-here terrain.' A several-hundred-foot-long chasm (possibly a fault) cuts across the lower ridge, and the party ultimately had to find a break in a final cliff band and a scree slope to reach Pickell Pass; one partner chose to rappel sections that the other downclimbed.

set.approach: Mount Crowder has no trailhead and no maintained trail — every ascent is layered onto a multi-day, off-trail traverse through the heart of the Picket Range, and Crowder is almost never climbed as a standalone objective. Parties reach it via one of two corridors. From the south: the Goodell Creek climbers' path (turn off WA-20 opposite Newhalem into Goodell Creek Campground; the boot path starts behind a large boulder at the campground) climbs steeply and brushily through slide alder and old-growth timber, gaining roughly 2,500 ft in about a mile to reach the basins below McMillan Spire/Inspiration Peak in the Southern Pickets; from there it's a rugged, unmarked cross-country traverse north over intervening cols (Crescent Creek Basin, the shoulder east of Mount Terror, and bypasses around the McMillan Cirque "Barrier") toward the range's central saddle area. From the north/east: the Big Beaver Trail out of the Ross Dam trailhead on Ross Lake (often shortened with the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver/Beaver Pass Camp), leaving trail to climb Access Creek — staying on its north-flank benches through semi-open forest to about 3,700 ft, where brush thickens and a faint, cairned climbers' path crosses to the south bank and continues to the open basin at the creek's headwaters (reliable water, good camping). From either entry, Crowder itself is gained by traversing the connecting ridge past Pioneer Peak and Phantom Peak to Wild Pass, a heather-and-talus notch overlooking the small tarn of Wild Lake just below; from the pass, cross open slopes to the col between Phantom Peak and Crowder, then climb the broad SW Flank — tersely put, "climb SW from the col" — up easy 2nd/3rd-class scree, heather ramps, and low-angle rock to the summit. There is no reliable water above Wild Lake, and the connecting terrain between passes is exposed talus and heather with genuine routefinding difficulty in poor visibility; expect several full days of off-trail travel carrying multi-day loads to even reach Wild Pass.
set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the SW Flank exactly as climbed: down the easy 2nd/3rd-class scree and heather ramps to the Phantom–Crowder col, then back over to Wild Pass above Wild Lake. This is a walk-off/downclimb on the standard route — no rappels are required. Do not be tempted to shortcut east off the NE Ridge toward Pickell Pass: a first-hand account found this alternative deceptively difficult — in practice descending it means weaving a convoluted line of grassy 3rd-class ledges broken by short, exposed 4th-class and even a couple of 5th-class downclimbing moves, past a major chasm/fault splitting the lower ridge, with an unprotectable vertical drop near the base that forced one climber in that party to rig an improvised rappel off natural gear (there is no fixed hardware anywhere on this peak) rather than downclimb it. On the standard SW Flank descent, plan on 0 rappels; a rope is not needed for the reversal, just careful 3rd-class scrambling technique and, ideally, a GPS track of your ascent line given the routefinding-heavy terrain.

set.beta: A 5.7 trad route (multi-grade string '5.7 / 5a / 15 / V+ / 13 / MVS / 4b') with a PG13 hazard rating, indicating some sparse/serious protection; detailed pitch-by-pitch beta has not been published anywhere accessible, unlike the well-recorded South Corner.
set.overview: A short, sporty pitch (5.7 PG13) on the northwest aspect of Cruiser's summit pinnacle, reached by continuing along the crest of Sawtooth Ridge past the South Corner start. It is a separate, established 1-pitch route alongside the 2-pitch South Corner — the mountain's only two recorded technical lines — rather than merely a variation encountered during a full Sawtooth Ridge traverse. Often combined with, or climbed as an alternate finish to, the South Corner during a visit to the ridge.

The classic and easiest technical line up Mount Cruiser (6,104 ft), the highest summit on the Olympic Mountains' Sawtooth Ridge and the objective most parties travel to the ridge for. From Needle Pass the route follows a Class 4 gully past a large chockstone ('Cannon Hole,' passed via a short squeeze/tunnel) to a broad, exposed platform. From the platform's end, a low-5th-class face pitch — variously rated 5.0 and 5.3 — leads to a belay on the summit ridge crest, followed by a short, very exposed Class 3 scramble to the true summit.

set.beta: Mount Dana's only recorded route is a straightforward scramble; it is classified simply as 'scrambling' with no formal class rating published, and it lacks the pitch-by-pitch detail that exists for the main Bailey Range Traverse peaks. Most parties reach the Bailey Range crest via the Elwha River Trail and travel off-trail; an alternate approach along the ridge from Mount Barnes to Dana reportedly involves exposed downclimbing, but this has not been formally written up. Treat this as a route-finding, self-sufficient objective rather than a beta-rich one.

This is rated 3rd class with only minor snow/ice difficulty; the glacier 'has experienced significant recession in recent years' but remains 'very reasonable' with good navigation and some scrambling. Early season, access the glacier via a snow finger on climber's right; late season, bypass via Class 3 scrambling left of the glacier. Cross the moat, ascend the upper glacier toward Mount Daniel's West Pyramid, and reach the col between the Middle and True summits.

set.overview: Mount Duckabush (6,232 ft) is a remote, multi-summit peak in the Skokomish–LaCrosse group of the central Olympic Mountains, within Olympic National Park's Daniel J. Evans Wilderness, on the divide between the Duckabush River headwaters and La Crosse Basin near Marmot Lake and O'Neil Pass. LIDAR survey data actually puts a subsidiary East Peak, about 3.4 miles NNE, roughly 7 ft higher (6,239 ft) than the traditionally-climbed main summit — parties chasing the true high point sometimes tag both. With only a handful of logged ascents on record, it's one of the least-visited named summits in the range, owing to an approach that runs 16+ trail miles one-way before any off-trail scrambling even starts.

Mount Fernow (9,249 ft) is the 8th-highest peak in Washington and the state's third-highest non-volcanic summit, capping the Entiat Mountains sub-range of the North Cascades within the Glacier Peak Wilderness, Chelan County. The headwaters of the Entiat River rise from its south slopes. It was first climbed in 1932 by Oscar Pennington and Hermann Ulrichs, and named by USFS supervisor Albert H. Sylvester for Bernhard Fernow, a pioneering 19th-century American forester. Fernow sits close to Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude, and the three are commonly linked into one trip from a shared Leroy Basin camp (locally nicknamed the 'Entiat 9ers'). The standard line climbs the broad south-facing terrain above Leroy Basin — called both the 'Southeast Face' and the 'Southwest Slope' — culminating in an exposed, loose summit block.

Mount Fricaba (7,139 ft) is a rain-shadowed, double-summit peak in the north-central Olympic Mountains, straddling the boundary between Olympic National Park and the Buckhorn Wilderness of Olympic National Forest — it is the highest point in both. It sits near Mount Deception and Mount Mystery and is composed largely of shattered Eocene sandstone, turbidite, and basaltic oceanic crust, producing loose shale and scree that make the climbing non-technical but tedious underfoot. First ascent 1957 by Don Bechlem (NE peak) and Jack Newman (SW peak). This entry covers the standard approach via Home Lake and Constance Pass into Deception Basin, gaining the peak's Southwest Ridge; an alternate approach climbs the Northeast Ridge directly from the Upper Dungeness River/Royal Basin side (crossing the river near ~4,400 ft, over Point 6138, along the ridge crest to the summit), often used as a loop with the SW-ridge line and covered by the 'Deception, Mystery, Fricaba & Hal Foss' scramble.

set.beta: The route rises straight out of Luna Cirque above Lousy Lake on the north side of Fury, starting from around 5,600 ft near the cirque floor. Begin on steep snow, then work into a couloir system - a bergschrund at the base often forces a rock bypass, and in late season that bypass has been reported as dirty 5.6 - and follow it toward the buttress crest, crossing snowfields exposed to rockfall from hanging glaciers above. Higher up, snow, rock and moats alternate and the route-finding is tricky, with protection not always where you want it; near the crest a slabby step of about 5.9 is the technical crux, after which an airy but easier traverse around the right side of the ridge leads to a snow arete running to the summit. One party reached the ridge crest in about 4.5 hours from a camp at 4,000 ft in Luna Cirque. Alan Kearney, who repeated it in September 1992 with Mark Price, noted that the late season made for much more rock climbing down low, since Beckey and Davis in July 1962 climbed a lot of snow and avoided most of the rock.
set.approach: Two very different ways in, both serious. The usual modern approach mirrors the Luna Col approach and then drops over the back: SR 20 to the Ross Dam trailhead, a mile of trail to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, the Ross Lake Resort boat to Big Beaver Landing at about 1,600 ft, then 10-11.5 miles of Big Beaver Creek Trail past 39 Mile Camp to Luna Camp, another mile or so to the marked cut-off, a log crossing of Big Beaver Creek just north of Access Creek, and the Access Creek bushwhack (north bank through huckleberry, cross to the south bank near 3,800 ft where the brush pinches out) to Access Creek Basin at 4,300 ft. From there the scree chute to Access Col at 6,100 ft and the steep heather traverse to Luna Col at about 7,100-7,200 ft. From Luna Col descend north-northwest into Luna Cirque to Luna Lake at about 4,800 ft and continue southwest to a camp on the cirque floor beneath the buttress. The whole approach runs about 17 miles and 7,000 ft of gain from the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, and the descent from Luna Col into the cirque costs another 2,400 ft that has to be regained on the way out. Alan Kearney's party came in from the north instead, from Chilliwack Lake in Canada up the Chilliwack River Trail, over Whatcom Pass and across the Challenger Glacier before descending into Luna Cirque to camp at Luna Lake - a longer, higher and even more committing approach.
set.descent_text: The buttress is an ascent line only; the standard exit is over the top and down the other side. From the summit, downclimb the summit snowpatch (about 300 ft, 40 degrees at the base to nearly 50 degrees at the top - protect it with flukes or pickets, with the strongest climber first on belay) onto the Southeast Glacier, then descend the S-shaped snowfield past the bergschrund near 7,900 ft, keeping running belays where the gradient steepens and the runout is bad. Off the glacier, cross the rocky rib on the lower ledge, contour northeast through the talus basin, climb back up the heather chute to the northeast ridge crest, and follow the crest back over the terraced rock nose - one short rappel over the 25-ft step - to Luna Col. One traverse party instead descended the Southeast Glacier and continued toward Outrigger Peak and Picket Pass, which is the option if you are traversing the range rather than returning to Luna Col. Either way, a party that camped in Luna Cirque has to regain roughly 2,400 ft to Luna Col to retrieve gear and exit via Access Creek. Allow a full long day.

set.overview: Mount Hinman is a broad glaciated dome neighboring Mount Daniel (7,960 ft, less than 2 miles east). First climbed in 1928 and named in 1934 for Dr. Harry B. Hinman, a founding member of an Everett climbing club, the peak once carried two glaciers — Hinman Glacier on its north flank and the smaller Foss Glacier to the northeast — but Hinman Glacier was declared dead (no longer flowing) by 2022, and both are now reduced to stagnant, shrinking ice/snow patches. The standard route climbs from La Bohn Gap up the peak's north side, crossing the former glacier basins on now largely bare, unstable talus rather than true glacier ice.

set.approach: Start at the Lake Serene Trailhead (~600 ft) off Mount Index Road and follow the maintained Lake Serene Trail roughly 4.1 miles and about 2,000 ft of gain — passing the Bridal Veil Falls viewpoint spur around mile 1.6 — up to Lake Serene itself (~2,600 ft). At the lake, leave the maintained trail and pick up the unofficial climbers' path that traverses talus and large boulders along the west/south shore toward the base of North Index's imposing face; in early season this crossing goes over avalanche debris and lingering snow/ice piled at the lake's edge. The route then climbs directly up a brushy 'tunnel' on North Peak's lower face: steepening mossy slabs and 3rd/4th-class rock (often wet and downsloping, so treat as low-5th in practice) lead into thick brush with several vertical 10-20 ft steps of shrub-pulling before easier ground is gained on North Peak's upper ridge — this face section alone commonly takes many hours, with parties reporting barely reaching halfway up the face after 10 hours of climbing. From North Peak's summit the route continues as an exposed ridge traverse over the top of the Norwegian Buttresses to Middle Peak and on to Main/South Peak, with several notches along the way requiring careful downclimbing or short rappels to stay on route.

set.overview: Mount Lincoln (5,868 ft) is the second-highest summit on Sawtooth Ridge in the southeastern Olympic Mountains, on the shared boundary of Olympic National Park and the Mount Skokomish Wilderness (Olympic National Forest), Mason County. Its parent peak, Mount Cruiser (6,104 ft), sits 1.1 miles northeast; Lincoln has two sub-summits, North Peak (5,690 ft) and Southwest Peak (5,486 ft). Flapjack Lakes lie in a basin directly west/below the north sub-peak. The mountain is built of Eocene-age basalt from the same accretionary-wedge processes that formed the rest of the Olympics. First climbed in 1932 by Ken Soult and F.S. Harmon, Lincoln sees relatively few ascents (fewer than 30 logged) because the standard Flapjack Lakes approach involves notoriously tricky, unmarked route-finding.

set.beta: Mount Olson sees very few ascents. Most parties reach it as a side trip from the long Six Ridge traverse between the South Fork and North Fork Skokomish valleys: hike the South Fork Skokomish River Trail to Sundown Pass/Sundown Lake, join the Six Ridge Trail, then leave it on the primitive, unsigned way trail toward Mount Olson before finishing cross-country to the summit. There is no recorded roped climbing route, rack, or pitch-by-pitch description for this peak anywhere; it is treated purely as a bushwhack/scramble objective by Olympic peak-baggers.

Recorded only briefly as a 'difficult Bryan Burdo alpine rock climb' on Persis's north face — no detailed grade, pitch count, or topo is available. This is a serious, low-traffic line distinct from the peak's Class 2 West Ridge hiking route; treat it as an alpine rock objective requiring full trad rack, rope, and North Cascades route-finding/approach skills rather than a hiking route.

An abundance of small crags sits immediately above the trail between Stujack Pass and the summit, of which Pika Slab (5.0, trad, 2-star community rating) is the one named route. Detailed pitch-by-pitch beta, first-ascent info, and exact location are not published.
set.descent_text: There is nothing to descend from the slab itself beyond the short class 3 downclimb to the right. The real descent is the whole Northwest Ridge scramble in reverse, and that is where accidents happen on this mountain. Retrace the crest on the chipped ledges, taking the narrow ramp section slowly — hug the wall and stay constantly mindful of loose rock there. Reverse the class 3 rock step and the short chimney feature by facing in; on the descent the exposure feels considerably worse than it did going up, and although the terrain is only class 2-3 the drops on both sides of the knife-edge carry dire consequences. Multiple boot paths braid the upper ridge and they are not all equal, so pick your line rather than following whatever tread appears first. Recross the head of the permanent snowfield — early or late in the season this is the crux of the descent and where an ice axe earns its weight — then drop back into the notch at Stujack Pass. From the pass the trail is continuous but relentlessly steep; expect the switchbacks below the basin to punish knees for 2,400 ft down to Lake Metan, and then a further easy 1.5 miles of forest to the trailhead. Typical descent time from the summit to the car is 2-3 hours, and fast parties have done it in about 2.

set.approach: Drive to the White River Trailhead (also called the Indian Creek Trailhead) at the end of White River Road/FS-6400: from Leavenworth take US-2 west 15 miles to Coles Corner, turn onto SR-207 (Lake Wenatchee Highway) for 10.5 miles, then continue on White River Road/FS-6400 for a final 10 miles to the trailhead (2,300 ft). Follow the Indian Creek Trail north/west, crossing the White River and Indian Creek bridge, for roughly 4.5-6 miles. Near Airplane Creek, leave the maintained trail and bushwhack/scramble about 2,000 ft up to Airplane Lake (this leg runs 1.5-2 miles); from the lake, continue off-trail to the upper east slopes and summit via one of the three route options. Round trip is roughly 16 miles with about 5,300 ft of gain; a logged first-hand ascent recorded closer to 12 miles and 5,000 ft via a more direct Airplane Creek line, taking about 7.3 hours up and 4.4 hours down. From Airplane Lake, three lines reach the summit: the northeast ridge (working around a hidden, non-obvious cliff band north of the lake), a direct ascent of the clean upper east face slabs, or a looser steep-talus variation. Favoring the drainage about a quarter-mile downstream of Airplane Creek reportedly avoids the worst of the brush on the bushwhack in.

set.overview: Mount Seattle (6,246 ft) rises deep in the Olympic interior, about 7.5 miles southeast of Mount Olympus, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. Its northeast aspect drops over 3,800 ft to the Elwha valley in only about 1.5 miles, but the standard scramble routes stay on the gentler south/west scree and talus slopes. The peak was named April 29, 1890 by James Halbold Christie and topographer Charles Adams Barnes of the Seattle Press Expedition, in honor of the city that sponsored their winter crossing of the range; it was first climbed in 1907 by Asahel Curtis, Grant Humes, and Lorenz Nelson while reconnoitering for a climbing club's first attempt on Mount Olympus. Reaching the base of the peak requires a long, committing wilderness approach from either the Elwha or North Fork Quinault drainages — there is no easy day-trip line to this summit.

set.approach: Note: the Hanging Glacier/North Face approach lies in the White Salmon Creek drainage, one valley east of Price Lake, rather than on the Nooksack/Ruth Creek side with which it is sometimes grouped. Drive the Mount Baker Highway to Glacier, WA and get a free backcountry permit at the Glacier Public Service Center (required), then continue up the Salmon Ridge/Mount Baker Highway corridor to the small pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge site. Walk around the gate and follow the old road past the lodge site roughly a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. From there, with adequate snow cover, descend northeast off-trail to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier — this is where roped glacier travel typically begins, with crevasse hazard increasing through the season. Ascend the glacier and moraine to a bivy around 6,000–6,500 ft, below the first rock/ice barrier. From the bivy, traverse climber's left, above and across the hanging glacier that sits over Price Lake (visible below to the west) and beneath the upper hanging glacier tucked under the first rock barrier, to reach the base of the shoulder dividing the White Salmon and Price Glacier cirques (roughly 7,500–8,000 ft), where the technical climbing begins. Key hazards: brush/alder low in the White Salmon valley when the snowline has receded; open crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier; and, especially in early season, frequent avalanches shedding off the true North Face — parties are advised to stay right of it during the traverse rather than drifting left onto the face itself. An alternate approach used by some parties climbs the Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide to a bivy near the Lower Curtis Glacier, then descends about 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier and traverses the NW Rib to reach the base of the Hanging Glacier — an option from the standard Lake Ann/Fisher Chimneys trailhead rather than the White Salmon side.

set.beta: Follows the North Fork Skokomish River Trail from Staircase to First Divide (12.7 mi, climbing from about 785 ft to 4,688 ft), then leaves the maintained trail for cross-country Class 1 travel toward Mount Steel's summit (roughly 1,540 ft of further elevation gain; the exact off-trail distance and line beyond First Divide are not recorded).

set.overview: Mount Stickney (5,307 ft) sits on the ridge dividing the Sultan Basin from the Skykomish Valley near Index and Gold Bar, within the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest's Wild Sky Wilderness. It's a prominent, easily-recognized peak from US-2 eastbound but a deceptively involved outing: roughly 12-13 miles round trip with about 3,500 ft of gain, most of it on old logging road and a faint climbers' path through heavy brush before a short, steep, exposed gully leads to the summit ridge and plateau. Named for a prospector who worked claims in the area (it was earlier called Prospect Mountain).

The standard, non-technical route up Mount Stuart and the standard descent for every technical ridge/face route on the mountain. From the false summit (~9,200 ft) it's a short, exposed Class 2-3 scramble east along the ridge to the true summit. Fred Beckey called Stuart "without a rival as the crown peak in the central Cascades of Washington", and this route is the one most often photographed from Longs Pass.

set.beta: No separately named "North Face" route matching this grade (IV, 5.8, AI2) is known on the mountain. The north side is instead divided among the named North Ridge, Ice Cliff Glacier, Stuart Glacier Couloir, and Girth Pillar routes, plus the Lara Kellogg Memorial Route on the adjacent northeast face above Ice Cliff Glacier.

set.descent_text: Rappel/scramble the West Ridge to the Blob (The Rake)-Terror notch (2 rappels of ~30m), then descend a chossy, steep-snow gully with an overhanging chockstone rappel back into Crescent Creek Cirque. On the original ascent the return proved unexpectedly difficult, including a six-hour bushwhack after a barrier crossing went wrong.

There is no maintained trail off Mount Tom's summit — climbers reverse the ascent line rather than following a distinct down-route. Downclimb the loose class 3-4 summit block and connecting ridge back to the White Glacier/Hubert Glacier saddle, then rope back up for crevassed glacier travel back across toward the Snow Dome side of the Olympus massif; at least one party climbing Olympus with a Mount Tom side objective has described this reconnection as a 'steep and loose descent off the Olympus massif' that turned back an otherwise fit, motivated group — treat it as the technical crux of the day, not an afterthought. From there, continue down over Snow Dome and re-cross the crevassed Blue Glacier to the Lateral Moraine, descend the moraine trail to Glacier Meadows camp, and reverse the Hoh River Trail (re-crossing the fixed ladder at the mile-17.5 washout) back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route — there is no record of fixed rappel stations or rock rappelling anywhere on Mount Tom, and the easiest route is classed simply as 'glacier + class 3 scrambling.' Glacier sections require full roped-team glacier travel gear (harness, rope, crevasse-rescue kit, pickets) rather than rappelling gear. Given the loose, exposed class 3-4 downclimbing at the Tom-Olympus connection, some parties choose to belay or hand-line short sections here even though no fixed anchors exist — carry a rope and a light rack (slings, a picket or two, maybe a picket for an improvised anchor) for that purpose, not for rappelling.

set.approach: Start at the Tubal Cain Trailhead (elev. ~3,300 ft, reached via FR 2870/2880), and follow the Tubal Cain Trail #840 (Copper Creek drainage) south. The trail climbs gently through second-growth and old-growth conifer forest, gaining roughly 2,800 ft over the first ~5.5-6 miles. At about 3 miles, pass the signed junction with the Tull Canyon Trail #847 (a steep 0.6-mile side spur to a 1952 B-17 crash site) and continue straight on #840. Around 0.5 mile past that junction the trail crosses Copper Creek near the historic Tubal Cain Mine tailings (last reliable, easy water before the lake), then switchbacks up through subalpine meadows toward Buckhorn Pass. Watch for the unsigned or lightly-signed spur (near ~5,200 ft, roughly 5.5-6 miles in) that drops left/southwest to Buckhorn Lake -- it's easy to miss ('don't miss the left turn to Buckhorn Lake'). Follow this spur down to the lake, which is the last dependable water source before the summit push. From the south end of Buckhorn Lake the maintained tread disappears; cross the inlet stream/waterfall at the head of the lake and pick up a faint boot path heading southwest into avalanche-damaged timber (expect blowdown and light bushwhacking). This opens into a broad, flat bench of avalanche debris about 200 ft above the lake -- the true start of the off-trail scramble. From there climb a wide talus/scree gully trending south then curving east, breaking treeline around 5,800 ft (roughly 700 ft above the lake), where the going turns to loose rock and light class 2-3 scrambling. Angle east/southeast up increasingly loose slopes to gain the Iron-Worthington col at approximately 6,420 ft. Hazards on this leg: avalanche debris and blowdown near the lake, sustained loose scree/talus underfoot above treeline (helmet recommended for rockfall from parties above), and route-finding through the faint, unmarked path -- a GPS track or detailed written beta is strongly advised since cairns are sparse. From the Iron-Worthington col, angle northeast up open slopes to the base of Worthington's summit fin; the final class 3 scramble drops a few feet left of the ridge crest to a short (~10 ft) crack, then follows the top of the fin to the true summit.

set.overview: A 5-pitch, mostly-independent 5.9 line up low-angle ramps and corners on the same wall as Wright-Pond, joining that route's final two pitches to reach the top; recorded as a "partial new route" since its upper section repeats existing climbing.

set.beta: Approached from the NE Face base; climbs the arete proper at 5.6. Pitch count and precise length are not recorded — treat as a lightly-traveled, sparsely-protected alpine line.

The climbing is described as "hard and sustained" 5.9. A 2004 forum thread discusses whether chockstones in the chimney offer protection every 20-30 ft through the crux; no definitive answer was given, so treat it as a serious, sparsely-protected lead. Pitch count and length are not recorded.

Needle Peak sees very few ascents. The standard (and only reported) line leaves the unmaintained Swamp Creek Trail around 3,200 ft, climbs a steep brushy slope to gain the peak's long north ridge near 7,300–7,400 ft, then route-finds through west-facing gullies and krummholz along the ridge before a narrow, choss-filled Class 3 gully leads through stacked boulders to the summit.

set.approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of Hwy 20 (elev. ~5,400 ft), about one mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook and roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop. Follow the well-graded Blue Lake Trail southwest through subalpine forest. At about 1.4-1.5 miles, watch for a signed junction: the main trail continues straight toward Blue Lake, while a climber's path splits left/south, signed for "Liberty Bell Trail #727 – Climbing Access," reached just past a small stream/meadow that is the last reliable water source before the basin. Take the climber's trail, which switchbacks up through slabs, talus, and heather meadows into the Liberty Bell/Early Winters basin beneath the west faces of the spire group — roughly another 0.5 mile and 1,000-1,300 ft of gain, putting total approach distance at about 2 miles with 1,300-1,600 ft of gain from the car (most parties report 1-2 hours). From the upper basin, continue scrambling/traversing north along the base of North Early Winters Spire's west side, past the start of the West Face route, to a distinctive corner/crack system that leads to a tree-covered ledge — the shared start for the Northwest Corner and West Face. Hazards: lingering snow and occasional avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully well into June (many early-season parties boot or ski the lower approach), talus and slab sections with some route-finding among braided climbers' paths, and no dependable water once past the stream near the Liberty Bell Trail junction, so fill up there.

set.beta: Established in 2008 during an attempt to repeat the nearby 1993 Colorado Route, this line instead follows independent ground up the left side of the main north-face buttress system. It is one of at least four distinct technical lines on this face -- do not confuse it with the original 1979 Beckey-Nolting-Tindall north-face route or the 2017 'Drawbridge' (Zentler/Schilling), which climbs the central buttress directly below the summit. Rated 5.10d/6b+/E3 5b, Grade IV, with 3 stars.
set.overview: The North Face (Left Buttress) climbs a direct line up the left margin of Castle Peak's central north buttress, roughly 1,400 ft of granite with about half the pitches rated 5.10; the route follows clean cracks and corners low on the wall, then a distinctive yellow quartz dyke higher up to avoid dirtier rock, with generally solid, clean granite throughout.
set.descent_text: From the top of the route, descend via Castle Peak's east ridge to an obvious col, then down a snow finger back toward the approach glacier/basin, rather than reversing the climbing line.

This is a scramble route with no rappelling — a walk-off/downclimb via either the same ridge or a loop over the summit. Reversing the North Ridge directly is unpleasant: it's a chossy nightmare of loose, exposed 3rd-to-low-4th-class terrain in its final several hundred feet below the summit, and downclimbing it with a heavy overnight pack is considered the harder, riskier option even though it's shorter. Many parties instead descend via the South Spur side: continue over/near the summit and down the south ridge's exposed Class 3 crest to the south-facing snowfield, glissade or plunge-step down to Perfect Pass, then loop back to Whatcom Pass either via the low-orbit traverse around the peak's east side or by crossing the Whatcom Glacier when it's consolidated (treat as glacier travel — rope and crevasse-rescue gear in early season). This adds distance but trades loose downclimbing for straightforward snow. No fixed rappel anchors exist on the North Ridge itself, and rope use beyond an optional running belay on the chossiest step is not described; rappels = 0, though a party uncomfortable downclimbing the loose upper ridge could improvise a natural (rock horn/gear) anchor for a short rappel.

set.beta: A ridge-crest link between Cloudy Peak and North Star: from Cloudy Pass, scramble the ridge up to Cloudy Peak with expanding views toward Glacier Peak, Eldorado, and Buckner, on rock that is reasonably solid Class 4 with an option to keep it at Class 3. From Cloudy Peak, lose elevation and cross talus slopes to reach North Star, finishing on the same lichen-slicked Class 3-4 summit step as the standard route. Most parties descend directly toward the Cloudy Pass Trail (rejoining it around 6,300 ft) rather than re-climbing Cloudy Peak.

There is no independently named 'Olivine Scramble' route; North Twin Sister has a single standard line — the class 3-4 west ridge on the mountain's famously grippy, orange-weathered dunite. This entry is treated as the general scrambling description of that same route (the walk-up-oriented, unroped experience most parties actually have), while the sibling 'West Ridge' entry carries the more technical framing (mixed variation, roped sections). Expect sustained class 3 scrambling on exceptionally solid, high-friction rock, with short class 4 steps and multiple false summits near the top.

set.overview: A committing 1,800 ft, 9-pitch IV 5.9+ line up the lowest/leftmost corner of Sloan's West Face, first climbed by Mike Preiss and Mark Bunker in 2000, not 2020 as previously on file. After two funky, thinly-protected opening pitches you're essentially committed to finishing the route and descending the far side of the mountain.

set.beta: First climbed in 1952 (the same year Fred Beckey and Herb Staley first traversed Vasiliki Ridge), this route climbs an easy face on pitch one to a left-trending, rising ledge, continuing across the face to a sandy bench. Pitch two follows a slab with a good finger crack on its left side, well protected, leading directly to the summit. It is graded 5.4 (French 4a / UIAA IV) over 2 pitches totaling 240 ft.

Named for a falcon that swooped the first-ascent party on the exposed summit ridge, this route climbs roughly 700 feet of 4th/low-5th-class terrain up a left-trending gully system, then continuous 5.6-5.9 crack and groove climbing on sound gneiss to an easy, exposed final ridge pitch at the 7,225' summit. An earlier account frames the technical climbing as 8 named pitches (5.7-5.9) above 900 feet of talus; a more granular 15-pitch breakdown comes from later parties. Both accounts agree the crux is a steep 5.9 headwall roughly mid-route, and that while never desperate, the climbing is remote and demands solid alpine skills.

set.descent_text: The northwest face is the shorter of SEWS's west-side lines (6 pitches), and parties typically continue to the true summit and take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete (3rd/4th class with a short 5th-class step) to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (60m rope) from bolted anchors/chains down the gully to the base, returning via the climber's trail to Blue Lake Trail. There is no route-specific rappel-the-face option, so bailing mid-route would mean building natural gear anchors (pitons/cams noted in the route description) rather than relying on fixed hardware.

set.beta: This ridge was climbed by Sam Boyce and Kyle Willis in 2018 as one leg of their 'Boston Marathon' — a ~26.2-mile, mostly-soloed technical traverse circling the entire rim of Boston Basin (26 pitches up to 5.8 R, 26 rappels, 20,000+ ft of technical terrain). Their account calls this 'the likely unclimbed northwest ridge of Boston Peak,' describing 'deep... virgin choss' rated 5.5 X, including a two-pitch section climbed à cheval (straddling the ridge crest) across rock 'the consistency of feta cheese,' followed by roughly 1,000 additional feet of similarly poor climbing. It is accessed along the basin rim from the direction of Sharkfin Tower. There is no established description of this specific ridge as an independent route — treat it as an obscure, rarely-repeated line rather than a maintained trade route.
set.approach: There is no standalone approach described for this ridge. What is confirmed is that the ridge connecting Boston Peak toward Forbidden Peak passes over Sharkfin Tower (8,120+ ft), and the only known ascent reached it via a multi-day connecting traverse begun on Forbidden Peak rather than as a direct approach to Boston. For a party attempting it directly, the most logical line mirrors the standard access used for the Forbidden/Torment/Sharkfin ridge system: from the Cascade River Road pullout just past mile marker 22 (across from Johannesburg Mountain), follow the old mining road about 0.75 mile to the historic mine site, then the steep, eroded Boston Basin climbers' path — with four stream crossings — up through forest to treeline near 5,300 ft. Boston Basin proper sits at ~5,700 ft, with a low camp around 5,300 ft and a high camp around 6,400 ft. From high camp, glacier travel up the Quien Sabe/Boston Glacier basin toward the col between Sharkfin Tower and Boston would put a party at the low (southwest) end of this ridge; from there the crest itself has no published route description, so expect sustained, likely-loose 4th-class-or-harder ridge climbing with route-finding as the real crux. Treat this as a reasoned estimate from the area's standard access pattern, not confirmed beta for this specific line.

set.beta: The Northwest Ridge is the moderate line on Colchuck Balanced Rock and the route of choice for parties who want the summit rather than the west face's hard free climbing. The line gains an obvious gully from Colchuck Lake to the notch above Jabberwocky Tower, then third-class terrain leading to the ridge proper, followed by the sharp ridge at 5.6 to the summit. Total gain from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to the summit is about 4,760 ft, and a relaxed car-to-car time is roughly 12 hours. The final obstacle is the balanced summit block itself, a short boulder problem that most parties protect. Descent from the summit was a single 25 m rappel off an anchor down the east side, then scrambling talus around to the south saddle and back past Jabberwocky Tower to Colchuck Lake. The rock is granodiorite. The peak's first ascent was made in 1958 by Gene Prater and Thomas Quin, but that ascent is not attributed specifically to this line, so it is not recorded here as the route's first ascent.

An alternative to the West Side/Southwest scramble: from the LeConte Glacier, climb 2 to 3 pitches of easy/moderate class 5 rock directly up the peak's east side to the summit. It receives far less traffic than the standard snow-couloir-plus-scramble line, and no pitch-by-pitch grades or lengths are on record.

set.approach: There is no trail to this peak; the approach is the trip. From SR 20 just west of Newhalem, turn north opposite the North Cascades Visitor Center entrance road, go left at the immediate T-junction, past a gravel quarry, then right and uphill on a narrow but well-graded gravel road to the signed Goodell Creek climbers' trailhead (48.6733, -121.2658, about 600 ft).
