Follow the old roadbed up Goodell Creek for roughly 3.5-4 miles. At about 1,700 ft a stone arrow on the ground marks the unsigned turnoff for the Terror Creek climbers' path — it is easy to walk straight past it, so waypoint it in advance. From the arrow the boot-beaten path climbs relentlessly and steeply up the hillside, gaining about 5,000 ft with essentially no reliable water, to timberline at 5,000-5,200 ft. Above treeline make a rising traverse over meadows, slabs and snowfields toward a 6,200 ft saddle; the standard Terror Basin camp sits about 400 ft below the saddle at roughly 5,800 ft. One party took about 6.5 hours from the trailhead to Terror Basin. For Ottohorn you must keep going west: traverse Terror Basin holding roughly the 6,000 ft contour, then cross the Barrier — the ridge dividing Terror Basin from Crescent Creek Basin — at about 6,100 ft. The Barrier crossing is the non-technical crux of the whole trip: steep, loose, grassy 'serious Class 3' ledges where a slip is not survivable. Drop into Crescent Creek Basin and camp at about 6,200 ft (a good alternative camp sits at 6,400 ft on the Chopping Block ridge overlooking the basin). From that camp, snow and small glacier slopes lead northwest in about an hour to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col at roughly 7,400 ft, where the route proper begins. Note on the numbers: gainFt (7,240 ft) is the net trailhead-to-summit gain from recorded elevations; the Barrier crossing and the Terror Basin traverse add several hundred feet of extra up-and-down each way, and the near-identical Goodell Creek / Terror Basin / Barrier approach to Mount Terror is recorded at 20 miles and 10,000 ft round trip.

set.beta: There is no single defined 'route' up Oval Peak so much as a set of interchangeable Class 2 ridge/slope lines that all converge near the summit. Parties commonly approach via the West Fork Buttermilk Trail No. 411 or the Oval Creek Trail No. 410A/Eagle Creek Trail, leave the trail in the basin below the peak, and climb whichever ridge (east, southwest, or south) looks cleanest that day, often descending a different one for better scree/talus conditions. The peak is defined by talus — talus, talus, and more talus — with large boulders higher up. A popular variation links Oval with neighboring Star and Courtney Peaks via the Fish Creek Pass / West Buttermilk Ridge traverse.
set.overview: Oval Peak (8,800 ft) is the highest summit in the Sawtooth Range and in the Methow Mountains subrange of the North Cascades, and the high point of the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest. It rises between Lake Chelan and the Methow Valley, with roughly 2,730 ft of prominence and about 15.5 miles of isolation, making it one of the more prominent yet lightly-visited summits in the range. The peak is notorious among Washington scramblers for its talus — nicknamed the ruler of a talus-choked 'Chossdom' — and the main challenge is route-finding among the many similar-looking gullies and ribs on the upper mountain rather than any single hard move. It's frequently combined with neighboring Star and Courtney Peaks on a multi-day Sawtooth Ridge traverse out of Buttermilk Creek, but also stands on its own as an overnight or long day trip from the Oval Creek drainage.

Phantom Peak is a fittingly named, elusive summit of the Northern Pickets between Fury and the Challenger group, rimming the glacier-draped Luna Cirque. The Southwest Glacier–South Couloir–Southwest Ridge line — the peak's easiest way up (Class 4) — links a pocket glacier, a broken rock step, and a short exposed ridge crest to a summit with a deceptive false summit just below the true top.
set.descent_text: Standard practice is to reverse the ascent line rather than walk off a different way — there is no easy alternate descent gully on this peak. From the true summit, downclimb back across the false-summit ridge crest (using a hand line on the short, exposed step above the false summit if the party fixed one on the way up), then down the broken Class 2-3 rock slope to the top of the snow finger. This is also where you'll retrieve any snow flukes or pickets placed as running protection on the ascent — plan on down-climbing/down-tooling the snow finger and re-crossing the bergschrund via the same slabby rock step used going up. Below the bergschrund, descend the pocket glacier and snowfield back to the ~6,100-ft saddle in the southwest buttress, then reverse the ~1,000-ft traverse back to camp (Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine, if approached from Whatcom Pass) or continue down into the Luna Creek drainage to regain the brush and, eventually, the Big Beaver Trail. The one place real rappelling is recorded on this route is the short, steep summit tower/rock step just below the true summit: the 1959 second-ascent party (Josendal, Sharpe, Spickard) found downclimbing was not comfortable there and made two rappels down a roughly 150-ft cliff band on the east side of the summit ridge to get past it. Given the remote, rarely-visited, and reportedly 'somewhat rotten' rock in this gully/tower section, expect natural anchors only — slung horns or rock threads, not bolts — so carry a small rack of slings/cord for building anchors. A single 60m rope handles the two ~75-ft rappels comfortably (or two 30m/60m ropes if the party prefers not to pull and re-rig). Total descent time from summit back to a southwest-buttress base camp has been reported at around 5-6 hours by a party climbing this line. Overall hazard on descent is exposure and loose rock on the tower/gully sections, plus the same bergschrund and snow-finger objective hazards (crevasse fall, rockfall off the buttress walls) encountered on the way up, and — once back down in the trees — the same brutal, disorienting Luna Creek brush that makes the whole approach infamous.

set.beta: From the Lake Serene bathroom/toilet sign, leave the maintained trail and climb the west ridge above the lake — first across a brushy, boulder-strewn slope, then through rolling, partly-open forest — to the wooded summit. Accounts differ slightly on the exact off-trail distance (roughly 1.5-1.8 mi one-way), but agree on about 1,740 ft of additional gain above the lake. The terrain is Class 2 at worst but demands solid off-trail routefinding and is markedly easier when snow-covered.

set.descent_text: For the standard Class 2–3 scramble, the descent is the same gully used on ascent, back down to Pinnacle Saddle and out the maintained trail to Reflection Lakes — most parties downclimb the whole thing rather than rope up, and this is a walk-off/downclimb route, not a rappel route, in normal summer conditions. That said, the upper gully has a short, sustained Class 3 step with enough exposure that some parties choose to protect or rappel it rather than downclimb, particularly when the rock is wet or in early-season snow: a single ~40 ft rappel off a sling/natural anchor (block, horn, or small cam placement — there is no fixed/bolted anchor) gets you past the crux, after which the remaining scree gully back to the saddle is a straightforward downclimb. Carry a 30m or half a 60m rope and a few slings/small cams if you want this option in your back pocket rather than commit to a sketchy downclimb. Note this is distinct from the separate steeper winter/snow line up the same gully system (climbed with pickets, sometimes 1–2 short roped pitches near the top), which is descended by rappelling the gully on natural gear anchors — that is a different, more technical undertaking than the summer scramble covered here.

set.approach: Start at the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Trailhead (large lot at the end of FR 56). From the parking area, follow the Middle Fork Trail a short distance and cross the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River on the footbridge, then pick up the Pratt River/Pratt Connector Trail heading west/southwest — an easy, well-graded stretch of roughly 0.6 mile. Watch for the unsigned, unofficial Rainy Creek climbers' path branching off near the Rainy Creek crossing (easy to miss; GPS or a downloaded track helps here since it is not an official maintained trail). This boot path climbs steadily and steeply alongside Rainy Creek, crossing a couple of side streams/seasonal drainages around 3,100 ft — cross here rather than following the valley bottom, then angle south into steadily steepening forest to about 3,600 ft. Around 3,700 ft a short rock band forces a ~100 ft scramble move before you can side-hill in to Rainy Lake (3,800 ft), roughly 3.5-3.75 miles and 2-2.5 hours from the trailhead. The path is boot-trodden, muddy, and brushy in spots (salmonberry/blueberry brush and occasional blowdown), and largely disappears under snow through late spring — expect route-finding by feel/GPS above the lake. Rainy Lake itself is the last reliable water source. From the lake, leave the path entirely and climb the ridge that rises east then curves south above the lake's east shore, staying on the lake side (right/west side of the ridge crest) to skirt cliff bands near 4,200-4,800 ft; brushy at first, opening into slabby, mossy terrain and then open slopes above ~4,800 ft. Continue up to a flat bench with a small unnamed tarn at about 5,200 ft (this is the 'tarn/saddle' referenced on-file), then climb south to gain the summit ridge at a saddle around 5,800-5,924 ft with views down the whole Middle Fork valley, finishing with a short, straightforward ridge walk south to the 5,924 ft summit. Total is roughly 6-6.5 hours and 9.5-10 km (about 6 mi) one-way to match the ~19.3 km / 5,200 ft round trip; slab can be slick when wet, and cornices can build along the final summit ridge in winter/spring conditions.

set.beta: Primus Peak's difficulty lies almost entirely in its remoteness and glacier approach rather than technical climbing. The standard line (also called the 'East Slope') is 3rd class, with class 2-3 scrambling and moderate snow once above Lucky Pass. Most parties treat it as a 3-day trip with a high camp above Borealis Lake. A harder 'North Ridge' variant (5.6 trad, loose and exposed) exists for parties wanting technical climbing.
set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down-climb the summit talus back to the North Klawatti Glacier, rope back up, and re-cross the glacier (same crevasse-probing caution as the approach) to the base of the McAllister-Klawatti notch. Regaining the notch back up to Klawatti Col camp is normally a climb/scramble rather than a rappel; the technical crux of the day - the short ~50 ft step between the notch and the glacier - is the one spot parties commonly fix a hand line or short rappel on the way down from the ridge, then climb the same step (with a boost from a partner or a fixed line) on the return leg. Primus's west-ridge line has a similar ~8,200 ft notch requiring a roughly 50 ft rappel to regain the glacier when descending, which lines up with an account of a party rappelling at the McAllister-Klawatti col - treat this as a single, short technical rappel rather than a multi-pitch rap descent. A single 30-60m rope is more than sufficient (a doubled 30m or single 60m easily covers 50-60 ft); anchors are natural (slings on horns/blocks) rather than bolted, since this is remote glaciated terrain with no fixed hardware. From Klawatti Col camp, the multi-day exit reverses the approach: back across the Inspiration Glacier (whiteout and crevasse hazard again), down the Eldorado Glacier, through Eldorado Basin, down the boulder field and timber climbers' path, and back across the Cascade River to the trailhead. Watch for softening glacier bridges and increased rockfall/scree looseness on the boulder-field descent in the afternoon heat.

From the top of Solid Gold, most parties continue to easy ground and locate the shared 'Solid Gold' rap anchors (also used to descend Sail Away and other nearby lines) on the north side of the ridge. The standard descent is a single, full-length rappel — a 60m rope is typical — down the north face, landing on easier ground below; from there it's about a 30-minute scramble/downclimb east back around to the notch below the West Ridge and the base of the south face. Some parties instead break this into two shorter rappels from the same general anchor area depending on rope length and party size/gear drag. Anchors are natural (slung blocks/chockstones with webbing/tat), not bolted, and the anchors in this immediate area (shared with the West Ridge descent) have been periodically rebuilt and relocated as old tat accumulates — inspect and back up any station that looks worn.

set.beta: From the end of the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail, an unmaintained but cairned climbers' path continues up the long south ridge through forest, brush, and boulder fields to timberline. The route then traverses below steep cliffs on the peak's east side (prone to sliding) before climbing to the saddle between Pinnacle and Pyramid Peaks. From the saddle it's an easy walk to Pyramid's summit. The route's overall difficulty is Class 3 scrambling, though most of the elevation gain is Class 1-2 hiking with only short harder sections.

From a high camp at roughly 7,500 ft on the lower ridge, the route follows a long, stable, lightly-vegetated boulder ridge north of the summit. Two main gendarmes block easy passage; each is climbed at about 5.1-5.2 and then a rappel on the west side regains the ridge crest. The line appears sensible as a route; it sees very little traffic. Parties can bypass the technical sections by staying lower on the west slope, avoiding the vertical sections but missing the ridge's technical interest.

The North Couloir climbs continuous snow up Robinson's remote north face at a sustained 35-50 degrees, finishing with a short scramble to the summit ridge just below the top, where it joins the standard Southeast Ridge for the descent. A 2005 party found no register entries suggesting an ascent since 2003, underscoring how rarely it's climbed.

The finish of a longer cross-country ridge traverse rather than a stand-alone climb: from the Howard-Rock col, ascend Rock Mountain's northeast side (snow climbing and rock scrambling), then descend via the South Ridge-East Slope to the Rock Lake basin and exit on the standard Rock Mountain Trail. Requires solid off-trail navigation and, in early season, snow-travel skills (an ice axe was necessary on a June ascent).

set.overview: Ruth Peak (~6,850 ft; 6,841 ft on file here) is the third-highest summit in the Bailey Range, a remote sub-range of the northern Olympic Mountains, between higher neighbors Mount Carrie (6,995 ft, 0.9 mi NW) and Mount Fairchild (6,900 ft, 0.9 mi N). The Fairchild Glacier drapes its northeast slope. There is no trail to the summit — Ruth Peak sits deep in cross-country terrain south of the Sol Duc/High Divide country and is almost always climbed as a waypoint along the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse rather than as a standalone objective. First ascent 1961 by Bert Brown, Roy Etten, and Victor Nelson.

set.beta: Sentinel is most often climbed, probably almost exclusively climbed, by parties doing the famed Ptarmigan traverse. From a high camp near the LeConte–Sentinel col or on the South Cascade Glacier, parties ascend a slope to a moat on the right side of a ledge/ramp that crosses the south face; the ramp 'wasn't difficult but will keep you on your best behavior,' and the final section to the summit is straightforward Class 2-3 scrambling on snow and rock. A steeper variation exists via the west ridge, involving a steep snow ramp near 7,400 ft and a short low-5th-class rock step into a gully below the final ridge crest — this is harder than the standard line and should be treated as an alternate finish, not the default.

Descend exactly the way you went up (a bit of temporary flagging can help on the brushy class 3-4 terrain so you don't wander off-line), and do not reuse any old rappel webbing/tat found at the notch since it's likely to be years old — bring your own to replace it.
set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: descend the northeast ridge back toward the notch/saddle below the true summit, then downclimb or rappel the short class 3/4 technical step just below the summit. Most parties rappel this step — a single 150 ft rope covers both the lead and the rappel, and anything over 100 ft of rope is adequate for the ~100-150 ft rappel. This is a single rappel; no additional roped descents are reported lower on the route. Because Sheep Gap Mountain is an obscure, lightly-visited summit, no fixed bolted anchor is documented — expect to build or use a natural anchor (rock horn, chockstone, or sling around a block) rather than find bolts or chains, and bring gear/webbing to back it up or replace tat. From the base of the rappel, reverse the traverse back to Weden Pass, then retrace the talus/heather traverse and boot path down to Foggy Lake/Gothic Basin, and follow Weden Creek Trail #724 back down to Monte Cristo Road and Barlow Pass. Watch for loose rock on the class 3/4 terrain above and below the rappel and re-ford Weden Creek on the way out.

set.overview: Sherpa Balanced Rock is a ~20-ft granite obelisk perched on the crest of Sherpa Peak (8,605-8,630 ft, figures vary), a satellite summit of Mt. Stuart in the Stuart Range, Alpine Lakes Wilderness. It sits about 100 yards from Sherpa's true western high point; a sight-level survey found the block only ~2 ft lower than that summit, so many climbers consider tagging the block the true top of the peak. Dave Mahre, with Gene and Bill Prater, made the first ascent in 1955. Reaching the flat top requires a short, bold, historically-protected sequence off an overhanging pedestal.

set.beta: The route comprises three ridge sections separated by deep notches. The lower section is mostly class 2-4 terrain, commonly simul-climbed, staying just on the east side of the crest (harder climbing results if the crest itself is followed). After descending to the second notch, two 5.8 pitches (a dirty 5.8 chimney and a 5.8 crack pitch) lead toward the summit, separated by class 2-3 sections, with large detached blocks making protection difficult in places. A gendarme partway up offers the route's best technical climbing directly, or can be bypassed via a ~75-ft rappel to easier terrain west of the ridge.

From Boulder Basin (the standard base camp, ~5,500-6,000 ft), travel southeast onto the Sitkum Glacier and climb NE toward a saddle at roughly 9,500 ft just east of Sitkum Spire. From the saddle, follow the pumice Sitkum ridge toward Glacier Peak's summit, staying right of and slightly below the summit block, then move into a snow chute that leads to the top. Standard glacier travel gear (ice axe, crampons, rope, harness) is required; the overall line is Grade III, 'Easy Snow.'
set.overview: Sitkum Spire (~9,355 ft, ~92 ft of prominence) is a minor rock tower on the west summit ridge of Glacier Peak, about 1,200 vertical feet below Glacier Peak's true 10,541 ft summit. It is the obvious rock finger climbers pass just west of a broad saddle at roughly 9,500 ft while on the Sitkum Glacier / Boulder Basin route — the easiest and most-traveled line up Glacier Peak. Most parties treat the spire as a landmark and continue past it to Glacier Peak's summit rather than as a stand-alone objective, but its short class 4/low 5th rock finish can be tagged directly from the saddle by parties wanting the sub-summit itself.

set.beta: This entry corresponds to the same standard mountaineering line as the Corkscrew Route (routeId wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew) — the peak's standard route ascends the 'South Face and Upper West Face.' See that route's approach/beta for the full line; this entry's grade (Grade II, glacier/snow + Class 3 scramble) matches the Corkscrew Route, not the separate roped 5.7-5.8 technical 'West Face' rock route (first ascent Merrill-Minton), which is a distinct, much harder climb not reflected in the given grade/discipline data.

set.approach: Same NW-face approach as New York Gully via the Phantom Slide path. Pitch 1 starts in a corner roughly halfway between the Thunder Basin exit gully and the Snot Couloir; cross-reference New York Gully's approach beta and aerial photos of the face to find the start.

set.overview: The South Face is Pernod Spire's other established rock line, right of the 1952 Standard Route, first climbed by Peter Jewitt, Cliff Leight, and Dan Waters on July 10, 1988. It is rated 5.9 (HVS 5a) with a short A0 aid section on the original line.

Begins near the low-center of the south face at an obvious layback hand-crack (5.10, can be wet). Climb up and left to gain a rising ramp, then exit rightward in the upper section on fun 5.7-5.8 rock, topping out on the west ridge near the summit. Also cataloged as 'South Face Left', the FA is Mike Preiss & Don Preiss in 2004 — this resolves the previously uncertain FA year on file.

set.beta: The easiest of Concord's standard routes. Start with a class-2 walk across gravelly, gently down-sloping ledges to the first belay, then climb up and right toward trees. A roped scramble along the ridge crest leads to a sandy stance near a feature climbers call the 'shark fin.' The final pitch climbs up and over the shark fin and onto the summit block, belaying from bolts at the top. Rock quality and protection are good throughout.

set.overview: The most direct line up Inspiration Peak: about 600 ft (4 pitches) of clean rock, reached by crossing the glacier to a small buttress under the south face. Climb up and right to a right-trending ramp, belay below a corner system, then trend up and left to connect with the obvious 'Great Gash' — a chimney splitting the upper south face — and chimney to the top. First ascent party/date not known.

set.beta: Climbed by Fletch Taylor and Chris Dolejska on August 8, 1994 — the same day the pair also climbed Silver Star Mountain's northwest ridge, completing both routes within an 18-hour outing. Starting at the col between Vasiliki and Burgundy Spires with scrambling to a rightward-trending dihedral system below the south face, they instead stepped left onto fifth-class cracks: a single hand crack (5.7) leading to a finger crack (5.8+) and a belay. The second pitch climbs a 15-foot traverse left (5.9), then a widening finger crack (5.7) for about 50 feet to a large dihedral that leads to the summit. Described as a well-protected two- to three-pitch climb.

set.descent_text: From the south summit, traverse the connecting ridge to Guye's middle summit, then make a roughly 30-meter rappel from slung trees down to the north summit. From there, descend west via the Cave Ridge climbers' trail back toward Alpental, or alternatively east via the Commonwealth Basin trail — this is the shared standard descent for Guye Peak's south-side lines.

set.beta: The specific route details are not well documented. This route designation appears in the database but is not clearly distinguished from the Direct East Buttress (5.11a, 9 pitch variant).

set.overview: Effectively Luna Peak's standard technical line: from Luna Col/Luna Pass (reached via the Access Creek approach shared with the Southeast Slopes route), climb the broad south ridge on Class 2–3 talus to the false summit, then complete the exposed Class 3–4 traverse across the notch to the true (north) summit — the same crux described under the Southeast Slopes route. It is rated 4th class / 1 pitch, with an early-season ice/mixed component (M1) reflecting the snow and occasional verglas that can linger on the col and in the approach gullies into July.

set.descent_text: Do not reverse the North Ridge to descend — the standard guidance to bail out via the West Ridge instead is well founded: the last ~400 vertical feet of the North Ridge below the summit is steep, exposed low-5th-class terrain on the crest, and reversing it is slower and riskier than descending the standard line. From the summit, join/descend the West Ridge: follow the ridge crest down but do not stay glued to the crest proper through the steep section below the false summit — following the crest exactly can force an improvised rappel. Instead, contour off the crest to the right (north side) for roughly 200 yards from the false summit, losing about 500 ft, then cut back to rejoin the ridge crest lower down and follow the cairned scramble route down and left (south) to the base of the ridge near the 5,200 ft notch. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent for a party following the correct line — no rappels are required on the standard descent (rappels: 0), though carry a short rap setup as an emergency option if snow/ice conditions or a wrong turn onto the crest force a downclimb none of the party is comfortable reversing. Watch for loose rock and dirt in the bypass gully, and for a snow-filled moat at the base of the gully in early season. Once back down at the basin, retrace the approach: descend to Orsino Creek to refill water, pick up the climbers' path back through the talus and timber, and return to the bikes/logging road for the ride/hike out.

set.overview: South Twin Sister is the highest point of the Twin Sisters Range west of Mount Baker, rising from reddish-orange dunite/olivine rock — the largest exposed body of this ultramafic rock in the Western Hemisphere — rather than the granite and volcanic rock typical of the rest of the North Cascades. The West Ridge is the standard route and is widely regarded as some of the finest sustained scrambling in Washington: miles of solid, high-friction rock with steady Class 3-4 climbing and a short technical step where some parties choose to rope up.

set.descent_text: Descent is a combination of short technical rappels off the face followed by the shared Sharkfin descent gully used by all routes on the tower. From the top of the Southeast Face's second pitch, make two 75-foot (~23m) rappels back down to the notch atop Southeast Ridge pitch 1/2 - a single 60m rope doubled is more than adequate for both. The anchors here are bolted but sparse: the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 has no chains or rap rings, so plan to leave a locking biner, rap ring, or short cord unless you can retrieve gear on the way down; there is no anchor at the very base of pitch 1, so keep the team roped/attentive on that stretch. Once back at the ridge notch, continue down via the same downclimb-and-rappel gully system used to descend the Southeast Ridge (see that route's descent for detail) - expect several more short rappels on natural anchors (chockstones, boulders, occasional slung horns) interspersed with 3rd/4th-class downclimbing, dropping back onto the Quien Sabe Glacier and the walk back to camp. Loose rock in this gully is a real hazard, and this is where a well-documented, fatal accident occurred on July 10, 2005 (a party that had mistakenly entered this gully was retreating when a natural boulder anchor gave way about 10 feet into the rappel, sending three climbers and the boulder roughly 300 ft down the gully and killing them), so back up questionable anchors, rappel one at a time where the gully is confined, and don't over-trust a single boulder or flake.

set.overview: Named after the Neil Young song, Southern Man splits off from the Direct East Buttress about halfway up and climbs the south-facing headwall on SEWS's upper south side to the summit. First ascended by Mark Allen, Joel Kauffman, and Leaghan Falley, August 2008 (aided at 5.9+ C1); freed by B. Matthews and Bryan Burdo in 2010 at 5.11d (a September 2009 ascent by Burdo at 5.12a has also been reported but is unconfirmed — see data gaps).
set.descent_text: From the summit, take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete (3rd/4th class with a short, more exposed 5th-class section) to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (60m rope) from bolted anchors/chains down the gully to the base. Note that the belays on Southern Man itself are described as 'vague and not yet fixed' — this affects the climb, not the descent, but underscores that this route sees less traffic than the East Buttress it starts from, so don't expect a fully bolted rap line down the route itself if you need to bail from the upper headwall; natural anchors would be required there.

set.beta: From the saddle, hike/scramble up a mix of scree and loose rock roughly along or below the ridge, following the most-traveled line, to an obvious chute east of the western prominence. The chute climbs on increasingly steep, exposed but better-cleaned rock before topping out near the summit. It is rated 4th class with limited protection options — a few possibilities for slinging horns or trees near the top.

Most parties approach via Phelps Creek Trail to Leroy Basin, cross the Leroy High Route to Ice Lakes, camp at Lower or Upper Ice Lake, then descend and traverse into the basin between North and South Spectacle Butte before climbing the Southwest Ridge to the south summit. The line is a straightforward Class 3 ridge scramble, but the ridge crest is broken by loose gendarmes that force route-finding onto ledges and a short chossy chute/dike passage that some parties rate closer to Class 4.

Follows the standard approach to Headlee Pass, then crosses the talus toward Lake Elan/Vesper Lake and takes the first ramp up and right to the base of the South Ridge. The route climbs the ridgecrest with a brief detour onto its left side about halfway up: a ~200 ft, Class 4 first tower, then easier Class 2-3 climbing back to the ridgecrest, a 5th-class section (which is actually a downclimb off a block), then a couple more ropelengths of Class 3-4 to a false summit, and a couple more ropelengths beyond that to the true summit. Simul-climbing or moving unroped is recommended rather than pitching it out formally.
set.overview: A more technical, low-5th-class ridge scramble/climb on Sperry's south side - harder and more interesting than the standard route but without the commitment of the north/east face lines. It is heavily vegetated and "not a recommended route" for quality, though it is a real, documented line.

set.beta: An all off-trail alpine scramble of roughly 6 miles and about 5,000 ft of elevation gain from the FR63 roadside parking to the summit. Sustained bushwhacking and blowdown low down give way to a cliff-band bypass and a snow/scree gully, ending with an exposed, sometimes loose ridge scramble with two short sections of 4th/low-5th-class climbing where a rope is often carried. It is one of the least-climbed of the Everett-area Pin Peaks, and sees sparse recent traffic.

Fully bolted 100 ft (30 m) sport pitch rated 5.10b/c. The FA party (Wylie Moreshead) recommends starting left of the bolt line and straddling the low nose feature cheval-style rather than pulling straight onto it, keeping the rope managed on the inside leg to avoid an awkward twist. 12 bolts lead to chains at the top.

An alternate to the Southeast Ridge standard route: from the Boiling Lake area, a way trail contours below Martin and Switchback Peaks at roughly 7,200-7,300 ft; from there, climbers either pick up a boot path up the west face or climb the west ridge proper (class 2-3) to the summit. It sees far less traffic than the Cooney Lake/Southeast Ridge approach and is more commonly used by parties already in the Boiling Lake/Martin Peak basin as part of a larger Sawtooth Ridge traverse.

set.approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (2,300 ft, ~20-car lot with privy), follow the Barclay Creek Trail a short distance before leaving it to cross Barclay Creek — as of spring 2026 the footlog crossing has been removed for safety with no announced replacement, so expect a rock-hop or ford. Pick up an unmaintained climbers' path up Tailgunner Creek/Tailgunner Ravine; it's brushy with blowdown lower down and passes through a short waterfall ravine before reaching the base of the Tailgunner Couloir. Follow the couloir (steep snow in spring/early summer) to Tailgunner Pass at roughly 5,320-5,400 ft. The round trip is roughly 5-7 miles with 4,500-6,000 ft of elevation gain/loss depending on the exact line and whether Gunn Peak/Wing Peak are combined — budget a long day (8+ hours car-to-car) or plan an overnight camp near the pass.

set.overview: A short, exposed boulder problem atop the true summit of Colchuck Balanced Rock — climbing the balanced block itself. It is rated around V2 (5+ Font), about 12 ft tall, up the southeast crimpy arete.

set.beta: The traverse is 7 roped pitches (statically belayed, though simulclimbing is possible): fourth-class scrambling to a notch near 6,100 ft, a descent on steep snow into the Great Basin, moderate snow pitches on the east ridge, a sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side, mixed rock-and-snow sections with moat belays, and a final steep couloir ascent to the South Brother summit. The route is recommended north-to-south.

set.descent_text: No descent is separately documented for The Chalice. Because The Chalice shares its summit and a mid-face crossing ledge with Playing Not Spraying, the same SE-side rappel line is very likely used for both — this is an inference from the shared-summit/shared-ledge relationship, not a confirmed fact for The Chalice itself. Playing Not Spraying's first-ascent party rappelled the SE side of the peak on a single 70m rope, noting only natural anchors (trees, horns) and advising extra bulk webbing.

set.beta: Climbers approach via Goodell Creek and Terror Creek to a high camp on the Stump Hollow ridge below the peak, then climb 3rd/4th class terrain with a short section of low-5th-class rock (5.4) to reach the summit. Because the Pickets guard several summits from a shared basin, parties frequently combine this peak with Mount Degenhardt, Mount Terror, or Inspiration Peak on the same trip. Note: the peak's standard lines are most often described as a 'Northwest Route' (Class 4, traversing ledges on the north face between the NE and NW ridges) and a distinct 'Northeast Ridge' (5.5, 4 pitches) — both broadly consistent in character and difficulty with the historic South Route described here, but the label 'South Route' is not attached to any specific established line, so treat route-specific pitch/rappel counts with caution.

Fred Beckey reportedly attempted this face earlier and found it traumatic enough to never return, and historians called it a "Last Great Problem" that "should probably remain" unclimbed. Layton and Wolfe finally forced a route in 2005 after a brutal approach, climbing banded gneiss that offered very little solid protection; every hold reportedly required testing, and pitons often wouldn't set. Note: the grade/length is variously given as V+ 5.9+ A2- and ~2,500 ft, and as V+ 5.11- and 2,400 ft — the latter figures are used here, but treat the discrepancy as a sign of how approximate any grade is on this kind of loose, unrepeated wall.
set.overview: The Devils Club is a serious, remote Grade V alpine rock route up the roughly 2,000-2,500 ft east face of Southeast Mox Peak ("Hard Mox"), one of the most committing big walls in the Lower 48 given its approach. First climbed by Mike Layton and Eric (Erik) Wolfe over August 31-September 1, 2005, with one bivouac partway up the wall. Notably, the FA party topped out the East Face but — out of food and water — did not continue on to Southeast Mox's true summit; parties repeating the route should clarify whether their objective is the wall itself or the actual summit (which would require additional scrambling/climbing beyond the top of the face). A second-ascent party (Eric Wehrly, 2008) climbed a variation.

set.beta: The only documented established route to The Fin's summit is a single 120-ft pitch rated 5.4, known as 'The Fin--Northeast Face', first climbed by Harold Pinsch and Garry Tate in 1966. From the northeast side, angled bouldery moves gain a 'monster chimney' with good chockstones that feels more secure the deeper you go; an easy 3rd-class scramble from the top of the chimney reaches the true summit. Rock is pillow basalt — generally solid in the chimney but can be looser/chossier on the outer face, especially as the season progresses and snow melts off holds.

Ascends the south face starting in a small left-facing bolted dihedral; a highlight is a 5.11- slab traverse around pitch 5. Rated 3.8/5 by climbers with 182+ votes, considered a quality alpine trad testpiece alongside the neighboring Passenger and South Arete.

From Gladys Divide beyond Flapjack Lakes, the standard approach climbs a steep snow/scree gully to Needle Pass - icy and typically needing crampons and an axe into midsummer. A climbers'/goat trail then bypasses The Needle and Castle Spires along loose, exposed class 3-4 terrain to the notch south of The Horn. Do not underestimate The Horn as a simple scramble: despite the modest 5.5 grade, the final summit pitch is run-out and the rock demands careful gear placement.

Approach via the long Royal Basin trail to Upper Royal Basin, then leave trail to gain the Needles ridge crest and work along/among the summits to reach The Incisor. The peaks in the Royal Basin area are not walkups, and the terrain carries rockfall danger from rotten rock, though the Needles' rock is specifically higher quality than is typical for the Olympics. Expect Class 3-5.8 terrain somewhere on the massif depending on which line/summit is taken; no specific graded pitch count or line is established for The Incisor itself.

set.overview: The Rake is a serrated, ~7,869 ft summit in the Southern Pickets, on the ridge crest between Mount Terror and the McMillan/Himmelhorn group above upper Crescent Creek Basin. Its jagged, saw-toothed skyline — visible from the Terror Basin/Crescent Creek approach — gives the peak its name. The only documented technical route, the east ridge (IV 5.9), was first climbed July 26, 2003 by Mark Bunker, Colin Haley, and Wayne Wallace during their 'Walking the Fence' complete Southern Pickets enchainment. Nearly all recorded ascents of The Rake come as one leg of a larger Pickets traverse rather than as a stand-alone objective.

set.approach: Same trailhead-to-basin approach as the other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake Trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, take the maintained Snow Lake Trail ~1 mile (~700 ft gain) to Snow Lake for the last reliable water. Past the lake the tread fades over a wooded hump; contour up and right into the obvious NW-side talus/dirt gully, where a heather-bench climbers' path reappears near the top and drops you into the basin under the peak. Climb the moraine beside the small basin snowfield to the west saddle (Unicorn Col), then follow the traversing use trail below the summit cliffs, on the south side, to the base of the summit horn — total roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way and ~2,400 ft of gain. The Roof is the hardest and most exposed of the three summit-block lines (5.6, notably burlier than the Classic Route's corner and well above Open Book's 5.0), following a steeper, more sustained line up the south face; the top anchor for 'The Roof' is set back from the edge, meaning a cordelette/long sling is needed to extend the rappel power-point out to the lip — worth having a double-length runner for this reason even on the way up.
set.descent_text: Rappel is the standard descent off The Roof — downclimbing this line is considerably more exposed than reversing the Classic Route or Open Book given its steeper, more sustained character, so most parties rappel even if they scrambled up unroped elsewhere on the peak. The anchor is the same large rock horn used peak-wide on the south side of the summit block (not the old dead tree/snag, which is retired and unsound); it is set back from the edge, so extend it with a cordelette or webbing to keep the rope running cleanly over the lip and avoid rope drag/snagging on the roof feature itself. It's a single-rope rappel of roughly 40-50 ft to the notch/ground; 30m is commonly considered adequate, though some parties have found 30m marginal depending on which of the two rappel lines off the horn is used, so 40m removes the guesswork. From the base, reverse the traverse and basin/gully descent back to Snow Lake and out.

set.beta: No route on The Tooth is actually named 'Catscratch Couloir.' The physical description (NE-facing, winter ice/mixed line) matches the well-documented 'Northeast Slabs' route exactly, so the beta below describes Northeast Slabs. It climbs the NE-side slabs (originally graded around WI3, 50-70° ice on the first pitch, though conditions vary year to year), with a difficult-to-protect second pitch of thin ice and balancey mixed slab climbing, onto the North Ridge, finishing with a low-5th-class/M3 pitch over a notch on the east face before easier ground to the summit.
set.overview: This is the peak's documented winter/spring mixed line on the northeast side, generally referred to as the Northeast Slab (the name 'Catscratch Couloir' is not established for The Tooth, and does not appear in any coverage of this peak). It's a roughly 5-6 pitch snow/neve/ice/rock route close to the Alpental trailhead, giving a quick winter alpine outing when conditions are in — but the character swings widely year to year from good neve to bare rock and verglas.

set.beta: Climbed by Sam Boyce and Kyle Willis in July 2018 as part of a four-day 'Boston Marathon' link-up; they knew of no previously published complete west-to-east crossing. From Sibley Pass, a faint climbers' trail (generally used to access Marble Creek Basin) leads along the ridge; the route then tags West, Middle, and East Triad in sequence along the crest. The west face of Middle Triad has the best rock on the route and holds the technical crux at 5.6 R; elsewhere the ridge is serious, exposed 4th-class and low-5th-class scrambling on generally poor ('choss') rock. A separate 2018 descent of the East Ridge toward the Eldorado Glacier involved pushing past large loose blocks and roughly 500 ft of very exposed 5.6–5.7 downclimbing to reach the glacier.

set.descent_text: From the top, traverse south and west across broken 3rd/4th class terrain, losing elevation gradually until reaching a clean gully roughly 500 ft below the final belay. Descend the gully to a large ledge, then scramble southwest to walkable ground where you intersect the standard summit descent trail down to Aasgard Pass; follow the cairned, braided climbers' trail down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) back to Colchuck Lake, favoring climbers' left near the granite walls and watching for the common error of drifting climbers' right into cliffed terrain near Colchuck Peak. Crampons/axe are worth carrying into mid-summer for the Aasgard Pass snow. This is a walk-off descent - the route is not set up for rappel.

set.overview: A distinct line up Three Queens' Middle Peak (6,600 ft), climbing the south face to a rock gable below the summit and finishing up a class 4 chimney system; it has been climbed solo, car-to-car, as a day scramble/climb.

set.beta: The north face is 600 feet of class 5 granite climbing, first ascended by Bruce Garrett and Dennis Nelson on July 6, 1972. Little further pitch-by-pitch or modern beta exists for this specific line; it sees far less traffic than the popular SE-slope scramble or the nearby Slippery Slab Tower climb.

A Darin Berdinka route on Vesper's north face, one grade harder (5.8) than the neighboring Ragged Edge (5.7); it shares the same trailhead, basin, and col/ledge approach. Dedicated pitch-by-pitch beta is not available anywhere, so pitch count and exact line are unconfirmed beyond the FA record and grade.

set.descent_text: As a toprope wall, there's no rappel involved in normal use — climbers are lowered off by their belayer after each route. If you need to walk to the top to rig anchors, the walk-off is a short scramble around the back/side of the formation back to the base trail; this is not described in detail anywhere, so treat it as a standard short crag walk-off and scout it before committing a party to the top.

set.beta: Ascend along the SW spur, heading east to a broken ledge with a tree on the left. Climb up and left over a short slab to a notch, then through the notch and along a terraced ledge to a gully on the crest of the SW spur. Continue along the scree terrace below the summit block, then descend to the prominent tree visible from the road and climb the long crack to the summit.

This is a remote, non-technical scramble whose difficulty is really the approach: roughly 15-17 miles of biking/hiking one-way just to reach camp near Anderson Pass, followed by an 8-mile round-trip, ~4,000 ft scramble day with no maintained trail above the pass. The summit push itself is rated Class 2. There is no record of a notable first ascent or established named line — it is climbed as a cross-country objective, not a route in the rock-climbing sense.

Most parties approach via the historic Monte Cristo townsite and the Glacier Basin Trail, then leave the maintained trail to work up talus/scree toward the col ('moat') between Columbia Peak and Wilmans Peaks before gaining the northwest ridge for the final Class 4 scramble to the summit. This northwest ridge line is the peak's easiest route.

set.overview: Winchester Mountain is one of the most popular short hikes in the Mount Baker Wilderness, capped by a historic 1935 L-4 fire lookout that volunteers with the Mount Baker Club saved from demolition and restored in 1982; it has been open to the public for day use and first-come, first-served overnight stays ever since. The summit, reached via a steep but short trail from Twin Lakes, delivers 360-degree views across the Nooksack Cirque and Picket Range to Mount Shuksan and Mount Baker, and out to the jagged Canadian border peaks — American Border Peak, Canadian Border Peak, Mount Larrabee, The Pleiades, and Slesse Mountain — plus neighboring Tomyhoi Peak and Yellow Aster Butte.

set.beta: A third option to reach Windy Peak, starting near Hodges Horse Pasture at the Iron Gate Trailhead. The line follows the Boundary Trail (#533) north to Sunny Pass, then turns west to join the Windy Peak Trail for the final approach and the same Class 2 summit scramble used by the other two routes. It involves more ascent/descent along the way than the Long Swamp or Windy Creek approaches for a similar or shorter map distance.

This alternate ('Windy Peak via the Windy Creek Trail') cuts distance versus the Long Swamp approach by starting further west/higher along Toats Coulee Road. The Windy Creek Trail climbs to meet the upper Windy Peak trail network, then shares the same final easy scramble to the true summit. The trail is clear near the first creek crossing but has accumulated blowdown further along, so expect some deadfall to step over/around in less-maintained years.

set.approach: Same approach as the South Face route to Aasgard Pass (7,841 ft), then hike south toward the tower and ascend snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of the peak (roughly 6-8 hours and about 4,200 ft of gain from the trailhead).

set.beta: Follows the obvious scrub line traversing left under a small roof. Pull the roof on a good crimp, step right, and walk up the slab. Belay at a large dead tree just before the hiking trail. The climbing itself is 'crappy' but it offers a way up to the upper tier with less bushwhacking than the standard walk-off.
set.approach: From the Barlow Pass gate, walk the closed road (old railroad grade) approximately 4 miles to the Monte Cristo townsite; a backcountry campground sits at that mark. Mossy Loaf's coordinates place it essentially at/immediately adjacent to the townsite itself, so once at the flat of Monte Cristo the formation is only a short distance further off the main townsite path. The exact final spur to the specific wall isn't well described anywhere, so on-site scouting is recommended for the last stretch.
